title: Festivals
subtitle: The cycle of the Jewish year
intro: The Jewish year is a rhythm of memory, joy, and repentance. In this section you will learn how the calendar works, what happens on each holiday and fast, which mitzvot and customs are connected with them, and how the different movements of Judaism observe them.

overview.why: The Jewish year sets a rhythm of memory, joy, and repentance and teaches us to sanctify time: the first mitzvah given to the people already in Egypt was the sanctification of the new month. In every holiday the history of the people, the agricultural cycle of the Land of Israel, and the life of the home come together: candles, the table, a fast, or shared joy. One who goes through this cycle together with the community understands Judaism and begins to live it.
overview.examFocus: At the beit din, on the holidays they expect a story in your own words: how the calendar works, what you do on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, at the seder, in the sukkah, on Chanukah and Purim, and how you relate to fasts. They listen to see whether you understand why the mitzvah exists and whether you can say how you will fulfill it at home and in the synagogue according to your community's custom. Prepare a short anchor for each day: the Hebrew date, the main mitzvah, and your personal step.
goals: After this section you will be able to explain the Jewish calendar and the beginning of the day in the evening.
Tell what is done on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur: the shofar, teshuvah, and the fast.
Describe the sukkah, the four species, and how Simchat Torah is celebrated.
Explain chametz, the seder, and the link between Pesach and Shavuot through the counting of the Omer.
Name the mitzvot of Chanukah and Purim and the meaning of fasts and memorial days.

deeper.title: The Holidays in the Torah
deeper.text: Read Vayikra 23 and Devarim 16: they name Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Sukkot, Pesach, and Shavuot and say what is to be done on those days. From these chapters the lessons move on to custom and to the life of the home.

deeper.text: In “The Jewish World” by J. Telushkin it is convenient to see the holidays as a single cycle of the year. Read it alongside the lesson and check the meaning of each day against what has already been said in the section.

deeper.text: In the siddur “Vrata Molitvy” (“Gates of Prayer”) find the blessing over the shofar, “Unetaneh Tokef,” “leishev ba-sukkah,” the counting of the Omer, and the blessings of Chanukah. If your community uses a different siddur, look for the same texts and say them aloud.

deeper.title: The holidays in the Reform machzor and community
deeper.text: The machzor Mishkan HaNefesh and the siddur Mishkan T'filah show how progressive communities pray on the Days of Awe and on the holidays: the full meaning of the day, often the Israeli calendar (without the second day of the Diaspora), equality in the ritual. Check against the practice of your community — in ROOPI the composition of the services may differ.

lessons.title: The Jewish Calendar
keyIdeas: The Jewish calendar is lunisolar: months last 29 or 30 days, and the second Adar keeps Pesach in the spring.
In the 19-year cycle there are seven leap years; Purim is then celebrated in the second Adar, closer to Pesach.
Months are counted from Nisan, the month of the Exodus, and the year number changes on Rosh Hashanah, 1 Tishrei.
A day begins at sunset, so a holiday begins on the eve; twilight is a time of doubt.
In the Diaspora the second day is a custom of the fathers; Rosh Hashanah is two days everywhere, Yom Kippur one. Reform communities usually follow the calendar of Israel.

blocks.text: Time that can be sanctified

To celebrate the Jewish holidays, you first of all need to understand *when* they fall. The Jewish calendar differs from the familiar Gregorian one, so Pesach or Chanukah falls on different dates of the “secular” calendar each year, but always on the same dates of the Jewish calendar. Pesach is always 15 Nisan, Chanukah is always 25 Kislev. Knowing the calendar is not a technical detail but part of Jewish life itself: encoded in it are the history of the people, the agricultural cycle of the Land of Israel, and the spiritual tasks of each season.

The first mitzvah that the Jewish people received, still in Egypt on the eve of the Exodus, was the mitzvah of sanctifying the new month. The Torah says: “This month is for you the beginning of months.” The Sages saw a deep meaning in this: a free person disposes of his own time, and the first thing a liberated people is taught is to fill time with holiness.

blocks.he: הַחֹדֶשׁ הַזֶּה לָכֶם רֹאשׁ חֳדָשִׁים, רִאשׁוֹן הוּא לָכֶם לְחָדְשֵׁי הַשָּׁנָה
blocks.translit: Ha-chodesh ha-zeh lachem rosh chodashim, rishon hu lachem le-chodshei ha-shanah
blocks.ru: This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it is the first for you among the months of the year

blocks.text: The Lunisolar Calendar

The Jewish calendar is **lunisolar**. Its months are lunar: each begins with the new moon, and the lunar cycle lasts about 29.5 days. That is why a Jewish month has either 29 or 30 days. Twelve lunar months make a year of about 354 days — 11 days shorter than the solar year. If the calendar were purely lunar (like the Muslim calendar), the holidays would gradually “drift” through the seasons. But the Torah requires that Pesach be in the spring: “Observe the month of Aviv (spring) and keep Pesach” (Devarim (Deuteronomy) 16:1). So the lunar calendar must be coordinated with the solar one.

To achieve this, in some years a thirteenth month is added — a second Adar. Such a year is called a **leap year** (Heb. *shanah me'uberet*, “pregnant year”). In a cycle of 19 years, seven are leap years: the 3rd, 6th, 8th, 11th, 14th, 17th and 19th. In a leap year there are Adar I (*adar alef*) and Adar II (*adar bet*); Purim is celebrated in the second Adar, closer to Pesach.

In the era of the Temple and the Sanhedrin, the new month was proclaimed on the testimony of witnesses who had seen the new moon, and the decision to add a month was made by the court of the Sages. When conditions in the Land of Israel became too difficult, a permanent calculated calendar was introduced. According to tradition, it was published by the patriarch Hillel II around 359 CE (4119 from the creation of the world). Jews all over the world still live by this calculation to this day.
The months of the year

The Torah counts the months from spring: the first month is Nisan, the month of the Exodus. The counting of the years, however, is from autumn: the year's number changes on Rosh Hashanah, 1 Tishrei. The Mishnah says that the year has four “new years” for different purposes: 1 Nisan — for kings and for festivals, 1 Elul — for the tithe of cattle, 1 Tishrei — for years, the shemitah and the jubilee, 15 Shevat (according to the school of Hillel) — for trees (Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:1). The Jews brought the names of the months from the Babylonian exile; in the Torah itself the months are more often called by numbers.

items: Nisan (March–April) — Pesach
Iyar (April–May) — the Counting of the Omer, Lag BaOmer, Yom HaAtzmaut
Sivan (May–June) — Shavuot
Tamuz (June–July) — the fast of the 17th of Tamuz
Av (July–August) — Tisha B'Av
Elul (August–September) — the month of preparation for the Days of Awe
Tishrei (September–October) — Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Sukkot, Shemini Atzeret, Simchat Torah
Cheshvan, or Marcheshvan (October–November) — a month without festivals
Kislev (November–December) — Chanukah
Tevet (December–January) — the end of Chanukah, the fast of the 10th of Tevet
Shevat (January–February) — Tu BiShvat
Adar (February–March) — Purim; in a leap year — Adar I and Adar II

blocks.text: The day begins in the evening

In the account of creation it is said: “And there was evening, and there was morning — one day” (Bereshit (Genesis) 1:5). From this comes the rule: the Jewish day begins at sunset. Therefore all festivals and Shabbat begin on the previous evening: if the calendar says that Pesach falls on a Wednesday, it means the first seder will be on Tuesday evening. The day ends with the appearance of the stars of the following day (*tzeit hakochavim*). The interval between sunset and the appearance of the stars is called *bein hashmashot* — “between the suns”; this is a time of uncertainty, and halacha treats it strictly: Shabbat and the festivals are accepted early and ended with a margin.
Practical advice: get a Jewish calendar (a printed one or an app) for your city. The candle-lighting time and the end of the festival depend on latitude and change every week.
Rosh Chodesh — the head of the month

blocks.he: רֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ
blocks.text: “the head of the month,” the first day of the new month; a semi-festival

The beginning of every month is the minor festival of **Rosh Chodesh**. If the previous month had 30 days, Rosh Chodesh lasts two days: the 30th day of the old month and the 1st day of the new one. If 29 — one day. The Torah mentions the beginnings of the months among the days of joy, when trumpets were blown over the sacrifices (Bamidbar (Numbers) 10:10). Today, on Rosh Chodesh, the passage “Ya'aleh v'yavo” is added to the prayers, the “half” Hallel is read (the psalms of praise 113–118 with passages skipped), the Torah is read, and the additional Musaf prayer is recited. On the Shabbat before the new month, the synagogue announces when Rosh Chodesh will fall and blesses it (*Birkat HaChodesh*).

There is an ancient custom by which women on Rosh Chodesh refrain from some heavy household work. The Midrash explains it as a reward to women for not giving their jewelry for the golden calf. In our time, many women's Torah-study groups meet specifically on Rosh Chodesh.

Work is not forbidden on Rosh Chodesh, but it is customary to arrange a somewhat more festive meal. One who forgot to add “Ya'aleh v'yavo” to the Amidah in the morning or in the afternoon must repeat the Amidah; one who forgot in the evening does not repeat it, since in the era of the Sanhedrin the month was not sanctified at night (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 97).
The second day of the festival in the Diaspora

When the month was proclaimed on the basis of witnesses, the news of it reached distant communities from Jerusalem with a delay. The Jews of the Diaspora did not know for certain whether the past month had 29 or 30 days, and therefore observed every festival **for two days** — out of doubt. This is called *yom tov sheni shel galuyot* — “the second festival day of the exile.” It would seem that after the introduction of the calculated calendar the doubt disappeared. But the Sages of the Talmud ruled to preserve the custom: “Be careful with the custom of your fathers that is in your hands” (Babylonian Talmud, Beitzah 4b).

items: In the Land of Israel Pesach lasts 7 days (the festival days are the first and the seventh), in the Diaspora — 8 (the festival days are the 1st, 2nd, 7th and 8th).
Shavuot in Israel is one day, in the Diaspora — two.
Sukkot + Shemini Atzeret in Israel are 8 days; Simchat Torah coincides with Shemini Atzeret; in the Diaspora Simchat Torah is a separate, ninth day.
Rosh Hashanah lasts two days everywhere, including in Israel.
Yom Kippur is one day everywhere: fasting for two days in a row would be beyond human strength.

blocks.text: The Conservative movement on the whole keeps the second festival day in the Diaspora, although the Committee on Jewish Law of the Rabbinical Assembly recognized as valid a community's decision to observe one day; in practice this depends on the particular community.

differs.text: Reform Judaism, as a rule, observes the festivals according to the calendar of the Land of Israel: one day of Shavuot, seven days of Pesach, and in many communities Rosh Hashanah — one day. This is a conscious position: the second day is regarded as an institution that has lost its basis.

cards.front: What type of calendar is the Jewish calendar?
cards.back: Lunisolar: the months are lunar (29 or 30 days), and the year is reconciled with the solar year by means of an additional month.

cards.front: How many days are there in an ordinary Jewish year?
cards.back: About 354 days — 12 lunar months; this is roughly 11 days less than the solar year.

cards.front: Why is a leap year needed?
cards.back: So that Pesach always falls in spring (Devarim 16:1). In a leap year a second Adar is added.

cards.front: How many leap years are there in the 19-year cycle?
cards.back: Seven: the 3rd, 6th, 8th, 11th, 14th, 17th and 19th years of the cycle.

cards.front: In which Adar is Purim celebrated in a leap year?
cards.back: In the second Adar (adar bet).

cards.front: Which month does the Torah call the first?
cards.back: Nisan — the month of the Exodus from Egypt (Shemot 12:2).

cards.front: From which day does the year's number change?
cards.back: From Rosh Hashanah, 1 Tishrei.

cards.front: Who, according to tradition, published the permanent calculated calendar?
cards.back: The patriarch Hillel II, around 359 CE.

cards.front: When do the Jewish days begin, and why?
cards.back: At sunset: “And there was evening, and there was morning — one day” (Bereshit 1:5).

cards.front: What is “bein hashmashot”?
cards.back: The twilight between sunset and the appearance of the stars — a time of uncertainty, which halacha treats strictly.

cards.front: How many days does Rosh Chodesh last?
cards.back: One day, if the previous month had 29 days; two (the 30th and the 1st), if 30.

cards.front: What is added to the prayer on Rosh Chodesh?
cards.back: “Ya'aleh v'yavo,” the half Hallel, the Torah reading and the Musaf prayer.

cards.front: What is “yom tov sheni shel galuyot”?
cards.back: The second festival day in the Diaspora: it arose because of doubt about the date and was preserved as a custom of the fathers (Beitzah 4b).

cards.front: Which festival lasts two days even in Israel?
cards.back: Rosh Hashanah.

cards.front: How many days does Pesach last in Israel and in the Diaspora?
cards.back: In Israel — 7 days, in the Diaspora — 8.

differs.text: Reform communities in the Diaspora usually observe 7 days, as in Israel.

cards.front: What if you forget “Ya'aleh v'yavo” in the morning Amidah on Rosh Chodesh?
cards.back: You must repeat the Amidah; if you forgot in the evening — you do not repeat it.

cards.front: On which dates do Pesach and Chanukah always fall?
cards.back: Pesach is always 15 Nisan, Chanukah is always 25 Kislev. According to the other calendar, the dates change from year to year.

cards.front: Which mitzvah did the people receive first, already in Egypt?
cards.back: The sanctification of the new month: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months” (Shemot 12:2). A free people learns to sanctify time.

cards.front: Where did the months get names like Nisan, Tishrei and Adar?
cards.back: They were brought from the Babylonian exile. In the Torah itself the months are more often called by numbers.

cards.front: Which month has no festivals of its own?
cards.back: Cheshvan, also called Marcheshvan. It stands between Tishrei and Kislev.

cards.front: When do the Jewish days end?
cards.back: With the appearance of the stars, *tzeit hakochavim*. A festival begun in the evening is completed not at sunset but with the stars.

cards.front: What is done in the synagogue on the Shabbat before the new month?
cards.back: They announce when Rosh Chodesh will be and bless the month. This is Birkat HaChodesh.

cards.front: With what does the Midrash connect the women's custom of Rosh Chodesh?
cards.back: With a reward to women: they did not give their jewelry for the golden calf. Many lighten heavy work and study Torah.

cards.front: How many days of Shavuot are there in Israel and in the Diaspora?
cards.back: In the Land of Israel — one day, in the Diaspora — two. Yom Kippur is one day everywhere: two fasts in a row would be beyond human strength.

lessons.title: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur: The Days of Awe
keyIdeas: The Ten Days of Repentance — from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur; the shofar is blown on weekday mornings throughout Elul, and selichot begin at the end of Elul, among the Sephardim from the beginning.
The main mitzvah of Rosh Hashanah is to hear the shofar: tekiah, shevarim and teruah; in Musaf the sections Malchuyot, Zichronot and Shofarot are sounded.
This is a festival: a round challah, an apple with honey and other simanim; Tashlich by the water is a custom, not a Torah commandment.
Teshuvah — return: acknowledge the transgression, regret it, pronounce the viduy and resolve not to repeat it; alongside it are prayer and tzedakah.
Yom Kippur is a fast of about 25 hours and five prohibitions; it atones for sins against other people only after one has asked them for forgiveness.

blocks.text: Yamim Nora'im — the Days of Awe

The autumn festivals open with a period called **Yamim Nora'im** — “the Days of Awe.” It begins on Rosh Hashanah (1–2 Tishrei) and ends on Yom Kippur (10 Tishrei). Together these ten days are called *Aseret Yemei Teshuvah* — “the Ten Days of Repentance.” The preparation begins a month earlier: throughout the month of Elul the shofar is blown in the synagogue on weekday mornings, and from the end of Elul (among the Sephardim — from the beginning of Elul) the penitential prayers *Selichot* are recited.

The Torah itself speaks very briefly about the first day of the seventh month: it is a “day of blowing” (*yom teruah*, Bamidbar (Numbers) 29:1) and “a remembrance of blowing” (*zichron teruah*, Vayikra (Leviticus) 23:24). Tradition reveals the meaning: this is the day when the Almighty judges the world, and the day of the creation of man. In the Rosh Hashanah prayers, G-d is proclaimed King, and man accepts His authority upon himself.
The shofar

The main mitzvah of Rosh Hashanah is **to hear the sound of the shofar**, an animal's horn (usually a ram's). The mitzvah is precisely *to hear*, so the blessing is pronounced “to hear the voice of the shofar.” The blasts are of three kinds: *tekiah* — one long, even sound; *shevarim* — three broken “groans”; *teruah* — nine or more short, staccato sounds. By custom, the shofar is blown one hundred times in the morning in the synagogue. The Rambam wrote that the shofar seems to say: “Awake, you who sleep, from your sleep, remember your Creator and return!”

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם, אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ לִשְׁמוֹעַ קוֹל שׁוֹפָר
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, asher kid'shanu b'mitzvotav v'tzivanu lishmoa kol shofar
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, L-rd our G-d, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us to hear the sound of the shofar

blocks.text: The Musaf prayer on Rosh Hashanah is built around three themes: *Malchuyot* (the kingship of the Almighty), *Zichronot* (remembrance — G-d remembers His creations and His covenant) and *Shofarot* (the shofar at Mount Sinai and the shofar of the future redemption). Here also sounds the famous prayer “Unetaneh Tokef” with the main idea of the Days of Awe:

blocks.he: וּתְשׁוּבָה וּתְפִלָּה וּצְדָקָה מַעֲבִירִין אֶת רֹעַ הַגְּזֵרָה
blocks.translit: Uteshuvah utfilah utzedakah ma'avirin et ro'a hagezeirah
blocks.ru: Repentance, prayer and charity annul the evil decree

blocks.text: If the first day of Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat, the shofar is not blown that day — the Sages feared that a person might carry the shofar to an expert through the public domain and thus violate Shabbat. In that case the shofar is heard only on the second day.

differs.text: In many Reform communities Rosh Hashanah is celebrated for one day, and if it falls on Shabbat, the shofar is blown even on Shabbat.

blocks.text: Customs of the festive table and Tashlich

Rosh Hashanah is not a gloomy day: it is a festival, with a meal, wine and challah. In this period the challah is customarily baked round — as a sign of the cycle of the year — and dipped in honey rather than salt. A slice of apple is dipped in honey with the words: “May it be Your will to renew for us a good and sweet year.” Other *simanim* (symbolic signs-wishes) may also be on the table: a pomegranate — “so that our merits may multiply like the seeds of a pomegranate,” a fish's head — “so that we may be a head and not a tail,” dates, carrots, a gourd. The set of simanim differs among Ashkenazim and Sephardim. People wish each other: “Le'shanah tovah tikatevu” — “May you be inscribed for a good year.”

blocks.he: יְהִי רָצוֹן מִלְּפָנֶיךָ שֶׁתְּחַדֵּשׁ עָלֵינוּ שָׁנָה טוֹבָה וּמְתוּקָה
blocks.translit: Yehi ratzon milfanecha shetchadesh aleinu shanah tovah umetukah
blocks.ru: May it be Your will to renew for us a year good and sweet
blocks.ref: Siddur, the customs of Rosh Hashanah evening

blocks.text: On the first day of the festival, after noon, people go to a body of water where fish live and recite the prayer **Tashlich** (“you will cast”). The name is taken from the verse of the prophet: “And you will cast into the depths of the sea all their sins” (Micah 7:19). Some empty out their pockets, symbolically getting rid of their sins. If the first day falls on Shabbat, Ashkenazim postpone Tashlich to the second day. Tashlich is a custom, not a Torah commandment.
Teshuvah, tefillah, tzedakah

The word **teshuvah** is usually translated as “repentance,” but literally it means “return” — to G-d and to one's true self. The Rambam describes teshuvah as a process: acknowledge the transgression, sincerely regret it, express this before the Almighty (*viduy*) and firmly resolve not to repeat it. **Tefillah** is prayer, addressing G-d. **Tzedakah** is not just “charity” but “justice”: helping the needy is a duty, not a favor. The Shabbat between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur is called *Shabbat Shuvah*.

No intermediary and no one else's sacrifice is needed for atonement. The prophet says: “Take with you words and return to the L-rd… instead of bulls, the words of our lips” (Hoshea 14:3), and Yechezkel teaches that every person answers for himself (Yechezkel 18:20). A person has a *yetzer hatov* and a *yetzer hara* — inclinations toward good and toward evil — and is free to return. Judaism does not teach that all are born already guilty in such a way that only another's death can remove this guilt. Therefore the doctrine that forgiveness is possible only through faith in someone else's sacrifice runs counter to the very fabric of the Days of Awe: teshuvah, tefillah and tzedakah.

On the eve of Yom Kippur many observe the custom of *kapparot* — a chicken is circled over the head or, increasingly, money, which is then given to the poor. Medieval authorities already debated this custom: the Rashba and Rabbi Yosef Karo objected to it, while the Rema supported it. By custom, men immerse in the mikveh on the eve of Yom Kippur.
Yom Kippur — the Day of Atonement

blocks.he: כִּי בַיּוֹם הַזֶּה יְכַפֵּר עֲלֵיכֶם לְטַהֵר אֶתְכֶם, מִכֹּל חַטֹּאתֵיכֶם לִפְנֵי ה׳ תִּטְהָרוּ
blocks.translit: Ki va'yom hazeh yechaper aleichem letaher etchem, mikol chatoteichem lifnei Adonai tit'haru
blocks.ru: For on this day atonement shall be made for you, to purify you: from all your sins you shall be purified before the L-rd

blocks.text: Yom Kippur, 10 Tishrei, is the holiest day of the year; it is called “the Shabbat of Shabbats.” The Torah commands that on this day one should “afflict one's soul” (Vayikra 23:27), and the Sages explain this as fasting. The fast lasts about **25 hours**: it begins before sunset on the eve and ends after the appearance of the stars. The Mishnah lists five prohibitions of this day (Mishnah Yoma 8:1):

items: Eating and drinking
Washing (washing for pleasure)
Anointing with oils and creams
Wearing leather shoes
Marital intimacy

blocks.text: In addition, any work is forbidden on Yom Kippur, as on Shabbat. Children below bar and bat mitzvah age are exempt from the fast, as are the sick for whom the fast is dangerous: preserving life (*pikuach nefesh*) is more important than the fast. The sick, pregnant and nursing women should consult a doctor and a rabbi in advance.

A Mishnah teaching is of great importance: Yom Kippur atones for a person's sins against G-d, but it does not atone for sins against another person until the person asks the one he hurt for forgiveness and makes peace with him (Mishnah Yoma 8:9). Therefore it is customary on the eve of the festival to ask forgiveness from relatives, colleagues and acquaintances. On the eve of Yom Kippur there is a mitzvah to eat well; the last meal before the fast is called *seudah mafseket*.
The prayers of Yom Kippur: from Kol Nidrei to Neilah

The evening service opens with the solemn **Kol Nidrei** (“All vows”) — a text in Aramaic that is recited three times, even before sunset. This is a formula annulling the vows a person made to himself before G-d. It is important to understand: Kol Nidrei does not cancel promises and agreements with other people. The melody of Kol Nidrei is one of the most famous in Jewish music.

On Yom Kippur one prays five times: Maariv, Shacharit, Musaf, Minchah and the concluding prayer **Neilah** (“the closing [of the gates]”). In every service the confession *viduy* is recited — the short “Ashamnu” (“We have sinned”) and the long “Al Chet” (“For the sin…”). The confession is in the plural: the community answers for one another. Many dress in white; Ashkenazi men put on the white *kittel*. Neilah takes place when the sun is already sinking toward sunset. At the end everyone together recites “Shema Yisrael” once, “Baruch shem kevod malchuto le'olam va'ed” three times and “The L-rd, He is G-d” seven times; a long blast of the shofar sounds, and the community exclaims: “Le'shanah haba'ah bi'Yerushalayim!” — “Next year in Jerusalem!”
Right after Yom Kippur it is customary to begin building the sukkah, or at least to discuss its construction — so as to pass “from mitzvah to mitzvah.”

cards.front: What are the Yamim Nora'im?
cards.back: “Days of Awe” — from Rosh Hashanah (1–2 Tishrei) to Yom Kippur (10 Tishrei), the Ten Days of Repentance.

cards.front: How does the Torah call Rosh Hashanah?
cards.back: “Yom teruah” — the day of blowing (Bamidbar 29:1) and “zichron teruah” — a remembrance of blowing (Vayikra 23:24).

cards.front: What is the main mitzvah of Rosh Hashanah?
cards.back: To hear the sound of the shofar; the blessing is “lishmoa kol shofar.”

cards.front: Name the three kinds of shofar blasts.
cards.back: Tekiah — long; shevarim — three broken blasts; teruah — nine or more short ones.

cards.front: The three themes of Musaf on Rosh Hashanah?
cards.back: Malchuyot (kingship), Zichronot (remembrance), Shofarot (the shofar).

cards.front: Why is apple eaten with honey on Rosh Hashanah?
cards.back: As a sign-wish for a sweet year: “May it be Your will to renew for us a year good and sweet.”

cards.front: What is Tashlich?
cards.back: A prayer by a body of water on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, based on the verse “And you will cast into the depths of the sea all their sins” (Micah 7:19). A custom.

cards.front: What “annuls the evil decree” according to the prayer “Unetaneh Tokef”?
cards.back: Teshuvah (repentance), tefillah (prayer) and tzedakah (charity).

cards.front: What does “teshuvah” literally mean?
cards.back: “Return” — to G-d and to the right path.

cards.front: How long does the Yom Kippur fast last?
cards.back: About 25 hours: from sunset on the eve to the appearance of the stars.

cards.front: The five prohibitions of Yom Kippur?
cards.back: Food and drink, washing, anointing, leather shoes, marital intimacy (Mishnah Yoma 8:1).

cards.front: Does Yom Kippur atone for sins against people?
cards.back: No, not until the person asks the one he hurt for forgiveness (Mishnah Yoma 8:9).

cards.front: What is Kol Nidrei?
cards.back: An Aramaic formula annulling personal vows made before G-d at the beginning of Yom Kippur; it does not cancel obligations toward other people.

cards.front: What is the concluding prayer of Yom Kippur called?
cards.back: Neilah — “the closing [of the gates].”

cards.front: How does Neilah end?
cards.back: The Shema (once), “Baruch shem…” (3 times), “The L-rd, He is G-d” (7 times), the blast of the shofar and “Next year in Jerusalem!”

cards.front: Is the shofar blown if Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat?
cards.back: No — for fear of carrying the shofar on Shabbat; it is blown only on the second day.

differs.text: In many Reform communities the shofar is blown even on Shabbat.

cards.front: What is kapparot?
cards.back: A custom of the eve of Yom Kippur: a chicken or money is swung over the head and then given to the poor. Authorities debated the custom.

cards.front: When do Ashkenazim and Sephardim begin selichot?
cards.back: Ashkenazim — from the end of Elul, Sephardim — from the beginning of Elul.

cards.front: How many shofar blasts are sounded each morning?
cards.back: By custom, one hundred. Rambam saw the shofar as a call: wake up, remember the Creator and return.

cards.front: With what greeting is Rosh Hashanah welcomed?
cards.back: “Le-shanah tovah tikatevu” — “May you be inscribed for a good year.”

cards.front: What steps make up teshuvah according to Rambam?
cards.back: Acknowledge the wrongdoing, regret it sincerely, say vidui before the Almighty, and resolve not to repeat it.

cards.front: Who is not obligated to fast on Yom Kippur?
cards.back: Children before bar and bat mitzvah, and the sick for whom fasting is dangerous. Pikuach nefesh, saving a life, takes precedence over the fast.

cards.front: What is the confession on Yom Kippur?
cards.back: The short “Ashamnu” and the long “Al Chet.” They are said in the plural: the community answers for one another.

cards.front: What is customary to begin right after Yom Kippur?
cards.back: Building the sukkah or at least talking about building it, so as to pass from one mitzvah to another.

cards.front: What do many men do on the eve of Yom Kippur?
cards.back: They immerse in the mikveh. On that same eve there is the custom of kapparot: money or a chicken is given to the poor.

cards.front: Is an intermediary or someone else's sacrifice needed to receive forgiveness?
cards.back: No: the path to forgiveness is teshuvah, prayer, and tzedakah; “the words of our lips will replace the bulls” (Hoshea 14:3); each person answers for himself (Yechezkel 18:20).

cards.front: Does Judaism have an “original sin” that only someone else's sacrifice can remove?
cards.back: No. There is the yetzer hatov and the yetzer hara, and a person can return. Yechezkel 18:20: each person answers for himself.

lessons.title: Sukkot, Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah
keyIdeas: Sukkot from 15 Tishrei is the festival of pilgrimage: a remembrance of the huts in the desert and of the harvest, “the time of our joy.”
One lives in the sukkah for seven days; the s'chach is made of plants that grew from the earth and were separated from it, with more shade than sunlight.
The four species — the etrog, the lulav, the myrtle and the willow: taste is knowledge of the Torah, scent is good deeds; they bind different Jews together.
The Ushpizin are the righteous guests of the sukkah; they come where earthly guests are welcomed too, especially the poor.
Shemini Atzeret is a separate day with the prayer for rain; Simchat Torah is the end and the beginning of the Torah — on the same day in Israel, and on the next day in the diaspora.

blocks.text: The three pilgrimage festivals

Five days after Yom Kippur, on 15 Tishrei, begins **Sukkot** — the festival of huts. It is one of the three pilgrimage festivals (*shalosh regalim*), alongside Pesach and Shavuot: in the time of the Temple, Jews would go up to Jerusalem on these days. Sukkot lasts seven days; the first day (in the diaspora — the first two) is a full festival (*yom tov*), and the following days are *chol hamoed*, “the intermediate days of the festival,” when some work is permitted but the festive atmosphere remains. Right after Sukkot comes a separate festival — Shemini Atzeret.

Sukkot has two meanings. The historical one: a remembrance of how the Almighty settled the people of Israel in huts (or, in the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer in the Talmud, under “clouds of glory”) for forty years in the desert after the Exodus. The agricultural one: it is *chag ha'asif*, the festival of the harvest, when the fruit has been gathered from the fields and orchards. The Torah calls Sukkot a time of special joy: “And you shall rejoice in your festival… and you shall be altogether joyful” (Devarim (Deuteronomy) 16:14–15). Therefore in the prayers it is called *zman simchatenu* — “the time of our joy.”
The Sukkah

blocks.he: בַּסֻּכֹּת תֵּשְׁבוּ שִׁבְעַת יָמִים
blocks.ru: In sukkot you shall live for seven days

blocks.text: The main mitzvah of the festival is **to live in the sukkah**, a temporary structure under the open sky. “Live” means above all to eat there (especially bread and baked dishes), as well as to spend time and study — and, for those who can and whose community has such a custom, to sleep. The sukkah teaches humility and trust: a person leaves a sturdy house for a thin roof and remembers that what protects him is not stone but the Almighty. Before eating in the sukkah one says the blessing:

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם, אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ לֵישֵׁב בַּסֻּכָּה
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, asher kidshanu be-mitzvotav ve-tzivanu leishev ba-sukkah
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, L-rd our G-d, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us to sit in the sukkah

blocks.text: The most important part of the sukkah is its roof, the *s'chach*. It is made of plant material that grew from the earth and was separated from it: branches, reeds, bamboo, special mats. The s'chach must not be solid: by day the shade inside must exceed the sunlight, and at night one should ideally be able to see the stars through it. A sukkah is placed under the open sky, not under a tree or a balcony.

items: A sukkah must have no fewer than three walls (halacha permits two full walls and a third partial one); they are made of any sturdy material able to withstand an ordinary wind.
The height of a sukkah is no less than 10 tefachim (about 80–96 cm) and no more than 20 amot (about 9–10 m) (Mishnah Sukkah 1:1).
The s'chach may not be made of anything that can receive ritual impurity (processed products, utensils), nor of anything that did not grow from the earth (metal, plastic).

On the first night of the festival (in the diaspora — the second night as well) one must eat in the sukkah at least a kezayit (about 27–30 g) of bread; on the remaining days one may not hold a regular meal with bread in the house.
If it is raining and the food in the sukkah would be spoiled, a person is released from the sukkah: “one who suffers is released from the sukkah” (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 135).

blocks.text: The four species

blocks.he: וּלְקַחְתֶּם לָכֶם בַּיּוֹם הָרִאשׁוֹן פְּרִי עֵץ הָדָר כַּפֹּת תְּמָרִים וַעֲנַף עֵץ עָבֹת וְעַרְבֵי נָחַל
blocks.translit: U'lekachtem lachem ba-yom ha-rishon pri etz hadar kappot t'marim va-anaf etz avot ve-arvei nachal
blocks.ru: And you shall take for yourselves on the first day the fruit of a majestic tree, palm fronds, a branch of a leafy tree and willows of the brook

blocks.text: The second mitzvah of Sukkot is the **four species** (*arba minim*). The oral tradition explains the verse as follows:

items: **Etrog** (אֶתְרוֹג) — a citrus fruit, “the fruit of a majestic tree”; it has both taste and scent.
**Lulav** (לוּלָב) — a closed young branch of a date palm; the date has taste but no scent.
**Hadassim** (הֲדַסִּים) — three branches of myrtle; myrtle has scent but no taste.
**Aravot** (עֲרָבוֹת) — two branches of a willow; the willow has neither taste nor scent.

blocks.text: The Midrash compares the four species to four types of Jews: taste is knowledge of the Torah, scent is good deeds. There are people who have both, those who have only one, and those who have neither. The Almighty says: let all of them be bound together in one bundle, and they will atone for one another (Vayikra Rabbah 30:12). Thus the festival teaches the unity of the people.

The lulav, the myrtle and the willow are bound together. The bundle is held in the right hand and the etrog in the left (for left-handed people, the opposite, according to most opinions), the blessing is said, and then the species are waved (*na'anim*) in six directions — east, south, west, north, up and down — showing that G-d is everywhere. The four species are taken each day of Sukkot, except Shabbat.

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם, אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ עַל נְטִילַת לוּלָב
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, asher kidshanu be-mitzvotav ve-tzivanu al netilat lulav
blocks.ru: …who has sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us to take the lulav

blocks.text: In the synagogue, holding the four species, the congregation circles the bimah, saying the prayers *Hoshanot* (“Save, we pray!”). The seventh day of Sukkot, 21 Tishrei, is called **Hoshana Rabbah**: on this day seven circuits are made, and then a bundle of willows is beaten on the ground. By tradition, on Hoshana Rabbah the verdict pronounced on the Days of Awe is finally “sealed,” so many spend the preceding night in study.
Ushpizin — the celestial guests

According to the Kabbalistic tradition going back to the book of the Zohar, each evening high guests come to the sukkah — the **Ushpizin** (Aramaic for “guests”): Avraham, Yitzchak, Yaakov, Moshe, Aharon, Yosef and David, each on his own evening. They are invited with a special formula. The idea is simple and important: the righteous guests come only where earthly guests are welcomed too, especially the poor. Many communities also add “Ushpizot” — the matriarchs and prophetesses: Sarah, Rivka, Rachel, Leah, Miriam, Chana, Esther and others.
Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah

**Shemini Atzeret** (“the eighth day of assembly,” 22 Tishrei) is a separate festival right after Sukkot (Vayikra 23:36). The Midrash explains it as a request of the Almighty: “Stay with Me one more day.” On this day the Musaf begins to mention rain — the prayer *Geshem* — and from this time in the Amidah we say “who makes the wind blow and brings down the rain.” Ashkenazim read the memorial prayer *Yizkor*. In Israel Shemini Atzeret coincides with Simchat Torah; in the diaspora Simchat Torah is the next day, 23 Tishrei.

**Simchat Torah** — “the joy of the Torah.” On this day the annual cycle of Torah reading is concluded with the last portion of the book of Devarim and begun again at once with the first portion of Bereshit: the Torah has no end. All the scrolls are taken out of the ark, and the community dances with them around the bimah seven times — these are the *hakafot*. The one called up for the last passage is called *chatan Torah* (“bridegroom of the Torah”), and the one for the first passage of Bereshit — *chatan Bereshit*. Everyone is called up to the Torah, including children.
In the egalitarian communities of Masorti, women are also called up to the Torah; the honored roles of “kallat Torah” and “kallat Bereshit” are performed by women.

differs.text: In Orthodox communities only men are called up to the Torah; women take part in the celebration from their side of the synagogue, and in some communities separate women's hakafot are held.

In Reform communities of the diaspora, Simchat Torah is celebrated on Shemini Atzeret, as in Israel; women and men take part on equal terms. Often on this day children beginning their studies are honored.

cards.front: When does Sukkot begin and how long does it last?
cards.back: 15 Tishrei, seven days; Shemini Atzeret follows it.

cards.front: What is shalosh regalim?
cards.back: The three pilgrimage festivals in Jerusalem: Pesach, Shavuot and Sukkot.

cards.front: In memory of what do we live in the sukkah?
cards.back: Of how G-d settled Israel in huts (or under clouds of glory) in the desert (Vayikra 23:42–43).

cards.front: What is Sukkot called in the prayers?
cards.back: “Zman simchatenu” — the time of our joy.

cards.front: What is the s'chach and what is it made of?
cards.back: The roof of the sukkah, made of plant material that grew from the earth and was separated from it; more shade than sun.

cards.front: The blessing over food in the sukkah?
cards.back: “…ve-tzivanu leishev ba-sukkah” — who commanded us to sit in the sukkah.

cards.front: What height is permissible for a sukkah?
cards.back: No less than 10 tefachim and no more than 20 amot (Mishnah Sukkah 1:1).

cards.front: How much bread must one eat in the sukkah on the first night?
cards.back: At least a kezayit (about 27–30 g); this is an obligation.

cards.front: Must one stay in the sukkah in the rain?
cards.back: No: “one who suffers is released from the sukkah,” if the rain would spoil the food.

cards.front: Name the four species.
cards.back: Etrog, lulav (palm), hadassim (3 myrtle branches), aravot (2 willow branches) — Vayikra 23:40.

cards.front: What do the four species symbolize according to the Midrash?
cards.back: Four types of Jews (taste — Torah, scent — good deeds) bound together (Vayikra Rabbah 30:12).

cards.front: Are the four species taken on Shabbat?
cards.back: No, the four species are not taken on Shabbat.

cards.front: What is Hoshana Rabbah?
cards.back: The 7th day of Sukkot (21 Tishrei): seven circuits with the Hoshanot and the beating of willow branches; the “sealing” of the verdict.

cards.front: Who are the Ushpizin?
cards.back: The celestial guests of the sukkah: Avraham, Yitzchak, Yaakov, Moshe, Aharon, Yosef, David.

cards.front: Which prayer begins on Shemini Atzeret?
cards.back: The prayer for rain (Geshem); in the Amidah we say “who makes the wind blow and brings down the rain.”

cards.front: What happens on Simchat Torah?
cards.back: The Torah reading is finished and begun again at once; hakafot — seven circuits of dancing with the scrolls.

cards.front: Who are the chatan Torah and chatan Bereshit?
cards.back: Those called up to the last passage of Devarim and to the first passage of Bereshit on Simchat Torah.

cards.front: What two meanings does Sukkot unite?
cards.back: The memory of the desert huts — and, according to Rabbi Eliezer, of the clouds of glory — and chag ha'asif, the festival of the harvest.

cards.front: May a sukkah be placed under a balcony or a tree?
cards.back: No: the s'chach must be under the open sky. At night one should ideally be able to see the stars through the roof.

cards.front: How many walls does a sukkah need at minimum?
cards.back: No fewer than three. By halacha, two full walls and a third partial one suffice.

cards.front: In which hand is the lulav, and in which the etrog?
cards.back: The bundle is held in the right hand and the etrog in the left; for left-handed people, according to most opinions, the opposite. Then they are waved in six directions.

cards.front: Which blessing is said when taking the lulav?
cards.back: “Al netilat lulav” — the Almighty commanded us to take the lulav.

cards.front: Who are remembered as Ushpizot?
cards.back: The matriarchs and prophetesses: Sarah, Rivka, Rachel, Leah, Miriam, Chana, Esther and others.

cards.front: Are children called up to the Torah on Simchat Torah?
cards.back: Yes. Everyone is called up to the Torah, including children. In Orthodox communities only men and boys are called up.

cards.front: When do we begin the prayer for rain?
cards.back: On Shemini Atzeret, in the Musaf prayer. From then on we say in the Amidah: who makes the wind blow and brings down the rain.

lessons.title: Pesach, the Counting of the Omer and Shavuot
keyIdeas: Pesach, 15 Nisan, is “the time of our freedom”: chametz of the five grains is neither eaten nor kept; we eat matzah and tell of the Exodus.
At the seder we read the Haggadah, drink four cups and explain the pesach, the matzah and the maror; a person sees himself as having come out of Egypt.
From the second evening of Pesach we count 49 days of the Omer: freedom acquires meaning through the giving of the Torah.
Shavuot, 6 Sivan, is the time of the giving of the Torah; we read the Ten Commandments, many study all night and eat dairy foods.
On Shavuot we read the Book of Ruth: “Your people shall be my people, and your G-d my G-d” — the people and the acceptance of the faith.

blocks.text: The festival of freedom

**Pesach** begins on 15 Nisan and lasts seven days in the Land of Israel and eight in the diaspora. It is the festival of the Exodus from Egypt, the birth of the Jewish people. In the prayers it is called *zman cherutenu* — “the time of our freedom.” The name “Pesach” means “He passed over”: the Almighty “passed over” the Jewish homes during the slaying of the firstborn (Shemot (Exodus) 12:27). The main mitzvot of the festival are not to eat chametz and not to keep it at home, to eat matzah, and to tell the children of the Exodus.
Chametz

blocks.he: חָמֵץ
blocks.text: leavened food: a product of the five grains mixed with water and allowed to ferment

Chametz is a product of the five grains — wheat, barley, spelt, rye and oats — whose flour has been mixed with water and has had time to “rise.” Bread, cookies, pasta, beer, and most groats of these grains are chametz. On Pesach the Torah forbids not only eating chametz but also owning it: “For seven days no leaven shall be found in your houses” (Shemot 12:19). Matzah is dough of the same grains and water, baked quickly without letting it ferment; by halacha, no more than 18 minutes may pass from the mixing to the baking.

So before Pesach the house is thoroughly cleaned, and the dishes used all year are replaced with Passover dishes (or kashered, where possible). In spiritual terms, chametz symbolizes arrogance and a “puffed-up” self-importance, while matzah symbolizes simplicity and humility.

On the evening of 13 Nisan, with the arrival of the night of the 14th, **bedikat chametz** is performed — an inspection of the house by candlelight (today often by flashlight). Before the inspection the blessing “…al biur chametz” is said. By a widespread custom, ten wrapped pieces of bread are laid out in advance so that the inspection is not in vain. After the inspection the formula of nullification (*bitul*) “Kol Chamira…” is said in Aramaic: all chametz of which I am unaware shall be as the dust of the earth. On the morning of 14 Nisan, before the end of the fifth hour (by “halachic hours”), the remains are burned — **biur chametz** — and the formula of nullification is repeated for all the chametz. Chametz one is sorry to destroy is sold to a non-Jew through a rabbi (*mechirat chametz*) (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 111–114).

blocks.he: כָּל חֲמִירָא וַחֲמִיעָא דְּאִכָּא בִרְשׁוּתִי, דְּלָא חֲמִתֵּהּ וּדְלָא בִעַרְתֵּהּ וּדְלָא יְדַעְנָא לֵהּ, לִבָּטֵל וְלֶהֱוֵי הֶפְקֵר כְּעַפְרָא דְאַרְעָא
blocks.translit: Kol chamira va-chamiya de-ika birshuti, dela chamite u-dela vi-arte u-dela yedana leh, livateil ve-lehei hefker ke-afra de-ar'a
blocks.ru: All chametz and leaven in my possession that I have not seen, have not destroyed and do not know of — let them be nullified and become ownerless, like the dust of the earth

blocks.text: Ashkenazim by custom do not eat *kitniyot* on Pesach — legumes, rice, corn — while Sephardim do. In 2015 the Committee on Jewish Law and Standards of the Conservative movement permitted Ashkenazim to eat kitniyot, although many Conservative families keep the former custom.

differs.text: Orthodox Ashkenazim keep the prohibition of kitniyot as a binding custom.

blocks.text: The Seder

On the first evening of Pesach (in the diaspora — the first two) the **seder** is held — “order,” a festive meal with the reading of the **Haggadah**, the story of the Exodus. This is the fulfillment of the mitzvah “And you shall tell your son on that day” (Shemot 13:8). The seder is built as a lesson for children: it contains many unusual things so that the children will ask. The youngest asks the Four Questions, which begin with the words:

blocks.he: מַה נִּשְׁתַּנָּה הַלַּיְלָה הַזֶּה מִכָּל הַלֵּילוֹת
blocks.translit: Ma nishtanah halailah hazeh mikol haleilot
blocks.ru: Why is this night different from all other nights?

blocks.text: The seder consists of fifteen steps, which are customarily sung at the beginning:

items: Kadesh — kiddush over the first cup
Urchatz — washing the hands without a blessing
Karpas — a vegetable dipped in salt water
Yachatz — breaking the middle matzah; the larger part is hidden as the afikoman
Maggid — telling the story of the Exodus, the second cup
Rachtzah — washing the hands with a blessing
Motzi — the blessing over bread
Matzah — the blessing over the matzah and eating it
Maror — bitter herbs dipped in charoset
Korech — the “sandwich” of matzah and maror (the custom of Hillel)
Shulchan Orech — the festive meal
Tzafun — eating the afikoman
Barech — the blessing after the meal, the third cup
Hallel — psalms of praise, the fourth cup
Nirtzah — the conclusion: “Next year in Jerusalem!”

blocks.text: At the seder we drink **four cups** of wine or grape juice (Mishnah Pesachim 10:1). They are linked to the four expressions of redemption in the Torah: “I will bring you out,” “I will deliver you,” “I will redeem you,” “I will take you to Me as a people” (Shemot 6:6–7). We drink reclining on the left side, as free people did. Rabban Gamliel taught that one who has not explained three things at the seder — the **pesach** (the Paschal offering), the **matzah** and the **maror** — has not fulfilled his obligation (Mishnah Pesachim 10:5). Matzah is the bread of poverty and a sign of the hasty Exodus; maror (horseradish or bitter lettuce) is the bitterness of slavery; charoset (a mixture of nuts, apples and wine) recalls the clay from which the slaves made bricks. On the seder plate (*ke'arah*) lie also a roasted bone (*zeroa*) in memory of the Paschal offering and an egg (*beitzah*) in memory of the festival offering.
In every generation a person must see himself as if he himself had gone out of Egypt.

Every item of the seder is connected with the Exodus from Egypt. Matzah is the bread of poverty and haste, maror is the bitterness of slavery, the four cups are the four expressions of redemption (Shemot 6:6–7), the pesach is the memory of how the Almighty brought out our people. Sometimes people try to read the seder as a set of “secret signs” about a redeemer who has already come or about someone else's sacrifice. In the Jewish tradition the meaning of the evening is direct and open: “in every generation a person is obligated to see himself as having gone out of Egypt” (Mishnah Pesachim 10:5). This is the story of our exodus, not a cipher about another event.
The Counting of the Omer

From the second evening of Pesach begins the **Counting of the Omer** — 49 days until Shavuot (Vayikra 23:15–16). The omer is a measure of barley that was brought to the Temple on 16 Nisan. Each evening after the stars come out, the blessing is said and the count is announced: “Today is one day of the Omer.” The count links the freedom of Pesach with the giving of the Torah: freedom acquires meaning through responsibility. The days of the Omer are a time of semi-mourning in memory of the students of Rabbi Akiva, who died during this period (Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 62b): weddings are not held and hair is not cut; on which exactly these restrictions apply depends on the custom of the community.

blocks.he: הַיּוֹם יוֹם אֶחָד לָעֹמֶר
blocks.ru: Today is one day of the Omer
blocks.ref: Siddur, the Counting of the Omer

blocks.text: One who forgot to count in the evening counts during the day without a blessing, and on the following evenings — again with a blessing. One who missed an entire day continues counting without a blessing until the end (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 120).
Shavuot — the Giving of the Torah

**Shavuot** (“Weeks”) falls on 6 Sivan, the fiftieth day after the beginning of the counting; in the diaspora it is celebrated for two days. In the Torah it is the festival of the wheat harvest and of the first fruits (*bikkurim*), and tradition sees in it above all *zman matan Torateinu* — “the time of the giving of our Torah” at Mount Sinai. In the synagogue the Ten Commandments are read. Many stay awake all through the festival night studying Torah (*tikkun leil Shavuot*), decorate home and synagogue with greenery, and eat dairy dishes.
The Book of Ruth — the story of a giyur

On Shavuot we read **Megillat Ruth** — the Book of Ruth. For a person going through giyur, this is an especially close-to-home story. Ruth was a Moabite, the widow of a Jew. When her mother-in-law Naomi returns to the Land of Israel, Ruth refuses to leave her and speaks words that are regarded as the classic formula of accepting Jewishness:

blocks.he: כִּי אֶל אֲשֶׁר תֵּלְכִי אֵלֵךְ, וּבַאֲשֶׁר תָּלִינִי אָלִין, עַמֵּךְ עַמִּי וֵאלֹהַיִךְ אֱלֹהָי
blocks.translit: Ki el asher telchi elech, u-va'asher talini alin, amech ami ve-Elohayich Elohai
blocks.ru: Wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you lodge, I will lodge; your people are my people, and your G-d is my G-d

blocks.text: Ruth unites the two elements of giyur: belonging to the people (“your people shall be my people”) and accepting the faith and the commandments (“your G-d shall be my G-d”). Her great-grandson was King David (Ruth 4:17), and so Mashiach too descends from her. The book is read on Shavuot because the events take place at harvest time; because, according to tradition, David was born and died on Shavuot; and because the people's acceptance of the Torah at Sinai and Ruth's acceptance of the Torah are one and the same decision. The Sages said that at Sinai all of Israel, as it were, underwent giyur.
In many Reform communities, *confirmation* is held on Shavuot — a solemn ceremony for teenagers who have completed their religious education.

differs.text: Confirmation arose in the Reform movement in the 19th century; in some Conservative communities it has also been adopted, while in Orthodox communities there is no such practice.

cards.front: When does Pesach begin and how long does it last?
cards.back: 15 Nisan; 7 days in Israel, 8 in the diaspora.

cards.front: What is chametz?
cards.back: A product made from the five grains (wheat, barley, spelt, rye, oats) that has been mixed with water and leavened.

cards.front: What is forbidden on Pesach with regard to chametz?
cards.back: Eating it, as well as owning it and keeping it in the house (Shemot 12:19).

cards.front: Within what time must matzah dough not leaven?
cards.back: No more than 18 minutes from mixing with water to baking.

cards.front: What is bedikat chametz?
cards.back: The inspection of the home for chametz with a candle on the night of 14 Nisan, with the blessing “al biur chametz.”

cards.front: What are biur chametz and mechirat chametz?
cards.back: Biur is the burning of chametz on the morning of 14 Nisan; mechira is the sale of chametz to a non-Jew through a rabbi.

cards.front: What are kitniyot?
cards.back: Legumes, rice, and corn: Ashkenazim do not eat them on Pesach by custom, Sephardim do. In 2015 the Conservative Committee on Jewish Law and Standards permitted them to Ashkenazim.

cards.front: Which mitzvah is fulfilled at the seder by reading the Haggadah?
cards.back: “And you shall tell your son on that day” (Shemot 13:8).

cards.front: The first five steps of the seder?
cards.back: Kadesh, Urchatz, Karpas, Yachatz, Magid.

cards.front: What are the four cups of the seder connected with?
cards.back: With the four expressions of redemption: “I will bring you out,” “I will deliver you,” “I will redeem you,” “I will take you” (Shemot 6:6–7).

cards.front: Which three things must be explained at the seder according to Rabban Gamliel?
cards.back: Pesach (the sacrifice), matzah, and maror (Mishnah Pesachim 10:5).

cards.front: What do maror and charoset symbolize?
cards.back: Maror — the bitterness of slavery; charoset — the clay for the bricks.

cards.front: What is the afikoman?
cards.back: Half of the middle matzah, hidden at Yachatz and eaten at the end of the meal (Tzafun).

cards.front: How many days is the omer counted, and when does the counting begin?
cards.back: 49 days, from the second evening of Pesach (Vayikra 23:15–16).

cards.front: What should you do if you missed a full day of the omer count?
cards.back: Continue counting to the end, but without the blessing.

cards.front: When is Shavuot, and what is celebrated on it?
cards.back: 6 Sivan; the giving of the Torah at Sinai, the wheat harvest, and the first fruits.

cards.front: Which book is read on Shavuot, and why is it important for giyur?
cards.back: The Book of Ruth: Ruth the Moabite accepted the people and the G-d of Israel — “your people shall be my people, your G-d shall be my G-d” (Ruth 1:16).

cards.front: How is Ruth related to King David?
cards.back: She is his great-grandmother (Ruth 4:17).

cards.front: Where does the festival get the name “Pesach”?
cards.back: “He passed over”: the Almighty passed over the Jewish homes during the slaying of the firstborn (Shemot 12:27).

cards.front: How many pieces of bread are hidden before the inspection?
cards.back: By widespread custom, ten wrapped pieces, so that the search for chametz is not in vain.

cards.front: Until what time on the morning of 14 Nisan is chametz burned?
cards.back: Until the end of the fifth halachic hour. After that, the nullification formula is repeated over all the chametz.

cards.front: With what words do the Four Questions of the seder begin?
cards.back: “Ma nishtanah ha-laylah ha-zeh mi-kol ha-leilot” — “Why is this night different from all other nights?”

cards.front: What else is placed on the seder plate?
cards.back: Zeroa, a roasted bone, recalls the Passover sacrifice. Beitzah, an egg, recalls the festival sacrifice.

cards.front: What is the omer from which the counting begins?
cards.back: A measure of barley; it was brought to the Temple on 16 Nisan. From the second evening of Pesach, forty-nine days are counted.

cards.front: What is read on Shavuot, and how is the synagogue decorated?
cards.back: The Ten Commandments are read. Home and synagogue are decorated with greenery, and dairy dishes are eaten at the table.

cards.front: When, according to tradition, was David born and when did he die?
cards.back: On Shavuot. That is why the Book of Ruth, in which he is a descendant of a Moabite woman, is read specifically on this festival.

cards.front: What do the items of the seder speak about in Jewish tradition?
cards.back: About the Exodus from Egypt: matzah, maror, the four cups — a remembrance of how the Almighty brought our people out. These are not “secret signs” of some other redeemer.

lessons.title: Chanukah and Purim
keyIdeas: The Sages instituted Chanukah and Purim in memory of a miracle; work is not forbidden on them, and “Al ha-Nissim” is added to the prayer.
Chanukah lasts eight days from 25 Kislev, marking the dedication of the Temple; the cruse of pure oil enough for one day lasted eight days.
The lights are kindled to proclaim the miracle: from one candle to eight, plus the shamash; their light is not used for any purpose, and by custom women do no work while they burn.
Purim, 14 Adar, commemorates deliverance from Haman's decree; G-d's name is not mentioned in the book of Esther — the Almighty acts in hidden ways.
The four mitzvot of Purim: the Megillah in the evening and in the morning, mishloach manot, gifts to the poor, and the festive daytime meal.

blocks.text: Festivals instituted by the Sages

Chanukah and Purim are not mentioned in the Torah: the Sages and the prophets instituted them in memory of miracles that happened later. Therefore work is not forbidden on these days (although on Chanukah, by custom, women do not work while the candles are burning), but there are special mitzvot, blessings, and an addition to the prayer, “Al ha-Nissim” (“For the miracles”). Both festivals tell of the deliverance of the people: on Chanukah — from spiritual destruction, on Purim — from physical destruction.
The story of Chanukah

In the 2nd century BCE the Land of Israel was part of the Greco-Syrian Seleucid kingdom. King Antiochus IV Epiphanes, around 167 BCE, forbade the observance of Shabbat, brit milah, and the study of Torah, and set up an idolatrous cult in the Jerusalem Temple. Against him rose the priest Matityahu of the Hasmonean family and his sons; Yehuda Maccabee led the army. The few rebels defeated a powerful army, liberated Jerusalem, and on 25 Kislev 164 BCE cleansed and rededicated the Temple. The word “Chanukah” means “dedication, renewal.”

The Talmud relates: when the Hasmoneans entered the Temple, they found only one cruse of pure oil, sealed with the seal of the High Priest. It would have lasted one day, but the lamp burned for eight days, until new oil could be prepared. The following year the Sages established these days as a festival of praise and thanksgiving (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 21b). The Books of Maccabees, which tell of the war, were not included in the Tanakh but have been preserved in the Greek tradition.
The chanukiah: how to kindle

Chanukah lasts eight days, from 25 Kislev to 2 or 3 Tevet. The main mitzvah is **to kindle the Chanukah lights**, in order to “proclaim the miracle” (*pirsumei nisa*). The essence of the mitzvah is one candle each evening for the entire household, but all communities follow the most “beautiful” way of fulfilling it, according to the school of Hillel: on the first evening one candle is kindled, and each following evening one more is added, so that on the eighth evening eight are burning (Shabbat 21b). In addition, a helper candle — the **shamash** (“attendant”) — is lit, from which the others are kindled: the Chanukah light may not be used for anything, only watched.

items: The candles are placed from right to left: on the first evening — the far-right one; each evening a new candle is added to the left of the previous ones.
They are kindled from left to right: first the newest candle, then the others (this is the Ashkenazi custom according to the Rema; Sephardi customs differ in the details).
The chanukiah is placed at the entrance door, on the left side, opposite the mezuzah, or in a window facing the street, so that passersby can see the lights.
The lights must burn for at least half an hour after the stars come out.
On Friday the chanukiah is kindled before the Shabbat candles, using longer candles; at the end of Shabbat — after havdalah (at home).

blocks.text: Before kindling, blessings are recited. On the first evening a third blessing is added — “Shehecheyanu.”

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם, אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ לְהַדְלִיק נֵר חֲנֻכָּה
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, asher kidshanu be-mitzvotav ve-tzivanu lehadlik ner Chanukah
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, Adonai, our G-d, King of the universe, who sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us to kindle the Chanukah light
blocks.ref: Siddur, Chanukah (in some Ashkenazi siddurim — “ner shel Chanukah”)

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם, שֶׁעָשָׂה נִסִּים לַאֲבוֹתֵינוּ בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם בַּזְּמַן הַזֶּה
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, she-asah nissim la-avoteinu ba-yamim ha-hem ba-zman ha-zeh
blocks.ru: …who performed miracles for our ancestors in those days, at this time

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם, שֶׁהֶחֱיָנוּ וְקִיְּמָנוּ וְהִגִּיעָנוּ לַזְּמַן הַזֶּה
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, shehecheyanu ve-kiyemanu ve-higianu la-zman ha-zeh
blocks.ru: …who has granted us life, sustained us, and brought us to this time

blocks.text: Among Ashkenazim, every member of the family kindles the chanukiah (at least every man and boy); among Sephardim there is one chanukiah per household, which the head of the family kindles for everyone. Women are obligated in this mitzvah, “for they too were part of the miracle.” The best fuel is olive oil, but candles are also acceptable. The time for kindling according to the Shulchan Aruch is the emergence of the stars; according to other customs, at sunset (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 139).

Chanukah customs: in the prayers the full Hallel is recited all eight days; dishes fried in oil are eaten — latkes (potato pancakes) and doughnuts (*sufganiyot*); children play with the spinning top (*sevivon*, in Yiddish — *dreidl*) with the letters נ ג ה ש — “Nes gadol hayah sham,” “A great miracle happened there”; in Israel, instead of ש there is פ — “po,” “here.” It is customary to give children money — “Chanukah gelt.”
The story of Purim

Purim is celebrated on 14 Adar in memory of the events described in **Megillat Esther** (the book of Esther). In the Persian kingdom under King Achashverosh, the nobleman Haman obtained a decree for the destruction of all the Jews in a single day — 13 Adar; he chose the date by lot, *pur*, hence the name of the festival (Esther 3:7–13). Mordechai persuaded his kinswoman, Queen Esther, to intercede for the people. Before going to the king uninvited, at the risk of her life, Esther asked all the Jews to fast for three days (Esther 4:16). The decree was reversed: the Jews received the right to defend themselves, defeated their enemies on 13 Adar, and celebrated on the 14th, and in the capital, Shushan, on the 15th. Therefore in cities that were walled since the days of Yehoshua bin Nun (today this is above all Jerusalem), Purim is celebrated on 15 Adar — *Shushan Purim*.

In the book of Esther, G-d's name is never mentioned. Tradition sees in this the main lesson: the Almighty acts in hidden ways, through “coincidences” and through the decisions of people. The name “Esther” echoes the word *aster* — “I will hide.”
The four mitzvot of Purim

blocks.he: יְמֵי מִשְׁתֶּה וְשִׂמְחָה, וּמִשְׁלֹחַ מָנוֹת אִישׁ לְרֵעֵהוּ, וּמַתָּנוֹת לָאֶבְיֹנִים
blocks.translit: Yemei mishteh ve-simcha, u-mishloach manot ish le-re'ehu, u-matanot la-evyonim
blocks.ru: Days of feasting and gladness, sending portions of food to one another, and gifts to the poor

items: **Reading the Megillah** — twice: in the evening and in the morning. One must hear every word; at the mention of Haman's name it is customary to make noise with ratchets. The blessing is “…al mikra Megillah.”
**Mishloach manot** — sending at least one person a gift of two kinds of ready-to-eat food.

**Matanot la-evyonim** — giving gifts (money or food) to at least two poor people, one gift to each. The Sages taught that it is better to spend more on the poor than on the feast and on gifts to friends.
**Seudat Purim** — the festive meal on the daytime of 14 Adar, with wine and joy.

blocks.text: The Talmud says that on Purim one must drink “until one can no longer distinguish between ‘cursed is Haman’ and ‘blessed is Mordechai’” (Megillah 7b). Many authorities, including the Rema, explain: it is enough to drink a little more than usual and doze off. Drunkenness that leads to danger or to the transgression of other mitzvot is not a mitzvah. Children and adults customarily dress up in costumes, and on the eve, 13 Adar, the **Fast of Esther** is observed.
In Conservative communities, women read the Megillah for the whole community and count as fulfilling the mitzvah for others, just as men do.

differs.text: In Orthodox practice, women are obligated to hear the Megillah; whether a woman may read it for men is a matter of debate, and usually the Megillah for the community is read by a man, although women's readings for women also exist.

cards.front: When does Chanukah begin and how long does it last?
cards.back: 25 Kislev, eight days.

cards.front: Against whom did the Hasmoneans rise up?
cards.back: Against the Greco-Syrian king Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who had forbidden Shabbat, brit milah, and the study of Torah.

cards.front: What does the word “Chanukah” mean?
cards.back: “Dedication, renewal” — the Temple was rededicated on 25 Kislev.

cards.front: What miracle with oil is described in the Talmud?
cards.back: A cruse of pure oil enough for one day lasted eight days (Shabbat 21b).

cards.front: How many candles are kindled each evening of Chanukah?
cards.back: On the first evening one, then one more each evening, up to eight; plus the shamash.

cards.front: What is the shamash for?
cards.back: The other candles are kindled from it: the Chanukah light may not be used for anything, only watched.

cards.front: In what order are the candles placed and kindled (Ashkenazi custom)?
cards.back: They are placed from right to left and kindled from left to right — beginning with the newest candle.

cards.front: Where is the chanukiah placed?
cards.back: At the entrance door on the left, opposite the mezuzah, or in a window facing the street.

cards.front: Which blessings are said over the chanukiah?
cards.back: “Lehadlik ner Chanukah” and “She-asah nissim”; on the first evening also “Shehecheyanu.”

cards.front: What is kindled first on Friday during Chanukah?
cards.back: The chanukiah, and then the Shabbat candles.

cards.front: Who kindles the chanukiah among Ashkenazim and among Sephardim?
cards.back: Among Ashkenazim — every member of the family; among Sephardim — the head of the family, one chanukiah for everyone.

cards.front: What is written on the sevivon?
cards.back: נ ג ה ש — “A great miracle happened there”; in Israel פ — “here.”

cards.front: Where does the name “Purim” come from?
cards.back: From the word *pur* — the lot by which Haman chose the date for the destruction of the Jews (Esther 3:7).

cards.front: What is Shushan Purim?
cards.back: Purim on 15 Adar in cities that were walled since the days of Yehoshua (above all Jerusalem).

cards.front: Name the four mitzvot of Purim.
cards.back: Reading the Megillah (in the evening and in the morning), mishloach manot, matanot la-evyonim, and the festive meal.

cards.front: The minimum for mishloach manot and matanot la-evyonim?
cards.back: Mishloach manot — two kinds of food to one person; matanot — one gift each to two poor people.

cards.front: Whose name does not appear in the book of Esther?
cards.back: G-d's name: He acts in hidden ways, through events and people.

cards.front: Are Chanukah and Purim mentioned in the Torah?
cards.back: No: the Sages instituted them later. Work is not forbidden on these days; “Al ha-Nissim” is added to the prayer.

cards.front: What by custom do women not do while the lights are burning?
cards.back: They do not work while the Chanukah candles are burning. Weekday labor itself is not forbidden on Chanukah.

cards.front: Who led the Hasmonean army, and when was the Temple dedicated?
cards.back: Yehuda Maccabee, son of the priest Matityahu. The Temple was rededicated on 25 Kislev 164 BCE.

cards.front: What is the minimum of the mitzvah of the Chanukah light?
cards.back: One candle for the whole household each evening. According to the school of Hillel, one more candle is added each day, up to eight.

cards.front: Which Hallel is recited on all days of Chanukah?
cards.back: The full Hallel, without omissions, on all eight days.

cards.front: How is Esther's name connected with the hidden action of the Almighty?
cards.back: It echoes the word *aster*, “I will hide.” In the scroll, G-d's name is not mentioned: He acts through events.

cards.front: At what time of day is the Purim meal held?
cards.back: In the daytime of 14 Adar, not at night. On the eve, 13 Adar, the Fast of Esther is observed; many dress up in costumes.

cards.front: Are women obligated in the mitzvah of the Chanukah lights?
cards.back: Yes: “for they too were part of the miracle.” The best fuel is olive oil; ordinary candles are also acceptable.

lessons.title: Fasts and memorial days
keyIdeas: Fasts are a remembrance of calamities and a path to teshuvah; Zechariah names four fasts that will one day become days of joy.
Major fasts — about 25 hours, from sunset to the emergence of the stars the next day, with five prohibitions; minor fasts — from dawn, without food and drink.
Tisha B'Av remembers the destruction of the Temples and the exile from the Land; mourning is joined with hope for return and for the rebuilt Temple.
Tu BiShvat — the New Year of the Trees; Lag BaOmer, the 33rd day of the omer, is the day when the plague among the students of Rabbi Akiva ceased.
Yom HaShoah, Yom HaZikaron, Yom HaAtzmaut, and Yom Yerushalayim — days of remembrance and thanksgiving for the people, the Land, and the State of Israel.

blocks.text: Why do Jews fast

Besides Yom Kippur, the Jewish calendar has several public fasts. They are neither a punishment nor a “diet,” but a way to remember the catastrophes of the past and to reflect on one's deeds. Rambam writes that a fast should awaken the heart to repentance: what matters is not hunger, but inner change. The prophet Zechariah mentions four fasts — in the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months — and promises that in the future they will become days of joy and gladness (Zechariah 8:19). These are 17 Tammuz, 9 Av, 3 Tishrei, and 10 Tevet.
Two kinds of fasts

items: **Major fasts** — Yom Kippur and Tisha B'Av: they last from sunset to the emergence of the stars the next day (about 25 hours), and five prohibitions apply — eating and drinking, washing, anointing, leather shoes, and marital relations.
**Minor fasts** — 17 Tammuz, the Fast of Gedaliah, 10 Tevet, the Fast of Esther: they last from dawn to the emergence of the stars; only eating and drinking are forbidden.

blocks.text: The sick are exempt from the minor fasts, and by widespread practice pregnant and nursing women also do not fast; on Tisha B'Av they are required to fast unless there is danger — in each specific case one should ask a rabbi. If a fast falls on Shabbat, it is postponed: 17 Tammuz, 9 Av, and the Fast of Gedaliah — to Sunday, the Fast of Esther — to the preceding Thursday. The fast of 10 Tevet never falls on Shabbat in our calendar (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 121).
17 Tammuz and the “Three Weeks”

The Mishnah lists five calamities that befell on 17 Tammuz: Moshe broke the tablets upon seeing the golden calf; the daily sacrifice *tamid* ceased in the besieged Temple; the wall of Jerusalem was breached (during the siege of the Second Temple); Apostomus burned a Torah scroll; and an idol was set up in the Temple (Mishnah Taanit 4:6). From 17 Tammuz to 9 Av stretch *bein ha-metzarim* — the “Three Weeks” of mourning: no weddings or celebrations are held, music is not listened to, and many do not cut their hair. From 1 Av begin the “Nine Days” with further restrictions: Ashkenazim do not eat meat or drink wine, except on Shabbat; among Sephardim, some of the restrictions apply only in the week of Tisha B'Av.
Tisha B'Av

**Tisha B'Av**, 9 Av, is the saddest day of the year. According to the Mishnah, on this day it was decreed that the generation of the wilderness would not enter the Land of Israel (after the sin of the spies); the First Temple was destroyed (by the Babylonians, 586 BCE) and the Second Temple (by the Romans, 70 CE); the fortress of Beitar, the last stronghold of the Bar Kokhba revolt, fell; and Jerusalem was plowed over (Mishnah Taanit 4:6). Later tragedies are also associated with this day, for example the expulsion of the Jews from Spain in 1492.

In the evening, in the synagogue, by dim light, sitting on the floor or on low benches, the book of **Eichah** (Lamentations) is read, and in the morning — the elegies *kinot*. The book begins with the word that gave it its name:

blocks.he: אֵיכָה יָשְׁבָה בָדָד הָעִיר רַבָּתִי עָם
blocks.translit: Eichah yashvah badad ha-ir rabati am
blocks.ru: How lonely sits the city, once so full of people!

blocks.text: On Tisha B'Av, besides the five prohibitions, one does not study Torah (it gladdens the heart), except on sad topics — the book of Eichah, Iyov (Job), and the laws of mourning; people do not greet one another; until midday one sits on low seats. In the morning men do not put on tallit and tefillin — they put them on for the Mincha prayer (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 124).
The Second Temple was destroyed because of groundless hatred.

The grief of Tisha B'Av is over the destruction of the Temples and the exile from the Land. It is bound up with hope: the Temple will be rebuilt when Mashiach comes, whom we are still awaiting. Rambam writes that in those days these fasts will become days of joy and celebration (Laws of Fasts 5:19; Zechariah 8:19). That our people live again in Eretz Israel in our days is a true consolation; the very mourning over the Temple testifies that full redemption still lies ahead.
Tisha B'Av is a day of remembrance of all the tragedies of Jewish history and a day of reflection on the unity of the people.

differs.text: Classical 19th-century Reform Judaism did not mourn the Temple and did not pray for the restoration of sacrifices, so Tisha B'Av long went unobserved. Today many Reform communities mark it as a day of remembrance of catastrophes, with the reading of Eichah; fasting is a matter of personal choice.
Masorti observes the fast of Tisha B'Av; in some Conservative siddurim the wording of the 'Nachem' prayer has been changed to take into account that Jerusalem is now rebuilt.

blocks.text: The Fast of Gedaliah, 10 Tevet, the Fast of Esther

**The Fast of Gedaliah** (3 Tishrei, the day after Rosh Hashanah) — in memory of Gedaliah ben Achikam, the governor of Judea appointed by Nebuchadnezzar after the destruction of the First Temple. His murder by the Jew Yishmael ben Netanyah (Yirmiyahu 41:1–2) led to the flight of the remaining Jews to Egypt and the final desolation of the country. The Sages taught: the death of a righteous person is like the burning of the Temple. **10 Tevet** — the beginning of the siege of Jerusalem by the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar (Melachim II (II Kings) 25:1). In Israel this day has also been declared the Day of the General Kaddish — a memorial for the victims of the Holocaust whose date of death is unknown. **The Fast of Esther** (13 Adar) — in memory of the fast proclaimed by Esther; it was instituted later than the others and is considered lighter.
Tu BiShvat and Lag B'Omer

**Tu BiShvat** (15 Shevat) — the New Year of Trees (Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:1). Originally this was the date for counting the age of trees and the tithe on fruit. The Kabbalists of Tzfat in the 16th–17th centuries created the *Tu BiShvat seder* with fruits of the Land of Israel and four cups of wine. Today it is customary to eat fruits of the seven species for which the Land of Israel is famed (wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives, dates — Devarim 8:8), and in Israel to plant trees. Many communities see Tu BiShvat as a day of environmental responsibility.

**Lag B'Omer** (18 Iyar, the 33rd day of the counting of the Omer; the letters ל״ג give the number 33) — a day of joy in the midst of the mournful days of the Omer. According to tradition, on this day the plague among the students of Rabbi Akiva ceased; Kabbalistic tradition connects it with the day of the death of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, to whom the book of Zohar is attributed. Bonfires are lit, weddings are held, many Ashkenazim get haircuts (including the first haircut of three-year-old boys, the *halakeh*), and thousands of people come to Meron.
Yom HaShoah, Yom HaZikaron, Yom HaAtzmaut
