In the 20th century, days connected with the Holocaust and with the rebirth of the State of Israel appeared in the calendar. **Yom HaShoah** (27 Nisan) — Holocaust and Heroism Remembrance Day, established by the Knesset and connected with the Warsaw Ghetto uprising. At 10 a.m. a siren sounds in Israel and the whole country falls silent. **Yom HaZikaron** (4 Iyar) — a day of remembrance for the fallen soldiers and victims of terror: the price of the life of a people in its own Land. The next day, **5 Iyar**, is **Yom HaAtzmaut**, Independence Day: on 14 May 1948 (5 Iyar 5708) the State of Israel was proclaimed, and the Jewish people returned to sovereignty in its own Land. This is a day of thanksgiving. If these dates fall next to Shabbat, they are shifted so as not to violate Shabbat. **Yom Yerushalayim** (28 Iyar) marks the reunification of Jerusalem in 1967. Jerusalem is the eternal, undivided capital of the Jewish people; on this day many recite Hallel and thank G-d for returning to the Kotel.
How exactly one prays on these days depends on the custom of the community, but the meaning of the days is common: remembrance, thanksgiving, and connection with the Land of Israel.

items: In many communities — among religious Zionists, in Masorti, and in the Reform movement — the festive Hallel and special prayers are recited on Yom HaAtzmaut and Yom Yerushalayim. The Chief Rabbinate of Israel sees in the State the beginning of redemption.

Where the liturgy is not changed on these days, love of the Land and gratitude for the return of the people remain part of Jewish life all the same. This course teaches marking Yom HaAtzmaut and Yom Yerushalayim as days of joy, and Yom HaZikaron as a day of remembrance of the fallen.
In all movements, Yom HaShoah is a day of remembrance of the six million and of heroism; in some communities this remembrance also includes 10 Tevet and Tisha B'Av.

blocks.text: At the beit din interview you may be asked what the Land of Israel and the State of Israel mean to you. Answer in your own words: this is the Land of the covenant, Jerusalem is the eternal capital, Yom HaAtzmaut is a day of thanksgiving for the return of the people. How exactly one prays in your community — check with your rabbi; the very attitude toward the Land and toward Israel is part of the Jewish path, not an 'optional opinion'.

cards.front: Which four fasts does the prophet Zechariah mention?
cards.back: The fasts of the 4th, 5th, 7th and 10th months: 17 Tammuz, 9 Av, the Fast of Gedaliah, 10 Tevet (Zechariah 8:19).

cards.front: How do the major fasts differ from the minor ones?
cards.back: Major ones (Yom Kippur, Tisha B'Av) — from sunset until the stars appear, five prohibitions; minor ones — from dawn until the stars appear, only food and drink.

cards.front: Name the five calamities of 17 Tammuz.
cards.back: The tablets were broken, the daily offering (tamid) was discontinued, the wall of Jerusalem was breached, a Torah scroll was burned, an idol was placed in the Temple (Ta'anit 4:6).

cards.front: What are the 'Three Weeks' and the 'Nine Days'?
cards.back: The mournful period from 17 Tammuz to 9 Av; from 1 Av — the 'Nine Days' with intensified restrictions.

cards.front: What happened on 9 Av?
cards.back: The decree against the generation of the wilderness, the destruction of both Temples, the fall of Beitar, Jerusalem plowed under.

cards.front: Which book is read on Tisha B'Av?
cards.back: Eichah (Lamentations of Yirmiyahu), and in the morning — the kinot elegies.

cards.front: Why, according to the Talmud, was the Second Temple destroyed?
cards.back: Because of groundless hatred (Yoma 9b).

cards.front: When on Tisha B'Av are the tallit and tefillin put on?
cards.back: Not in the morning, but for the Mincha prayer.

cards.front: What does the Fast of Gedaliah commemorate?
cards.back: The murder of the governor Gedaliah ben Achikam after the destruction of the First Temple (Yirmiyahu 41:1–2); 3 Tishrei.

cards.front: What is remembered on 10 Tevet?
cards.back: The beginning of the siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar (Melachim II 25:1); in Israel also the Day of the General Kaddish.

cards.front: When is the Fast of Esther moved if 13 Adar falls on Shabbat?
cards.back: To the preceding Thursday.

cards.front: What is Tu BiShvat?
cards.back: 15 Shevat — the New Year of Trees (Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:1); fruits of the seven species are eaten, trees are planted.

cards.front: What is Lag B'Omer?
cards.back: The 33rd day of the Omer (18 Iyar): the end of the plague among the students of R. Akiva, the day of remembrance of R. Shimon bar Yochai; bonfires, weddings.

cards.front: When is Yom HaShoah?
cards.back: 27 Nisan — Holocaust and Heroism Remembrance Day.

cards.front: When are Yom HaZikaron and Yom HaAtzmaut?
cards.back: 4 Iyar — the day of remembrance of the fallen; 5 Iyar — Independence Day (1948).

cards.front: How does this course teach us to regard Yom HaAtzmaut?
cards.back: As a day of thanksgiving for the return of the people to its Land and for the State of Israel. In many communities Hallel is recited; love of the Land is part of the Jewish path.

cards.front: What is the main thing in a public fast according to Rambam?
cards.back: Not hunger itself, but an inner change: the fast must awaken the heart to repentance.

cards.front: Which later calamity is connected with the day of 9 Av?
cards.back: The expulsion of the Jews from Spain in 1492 — alongside the Temples, Beitar, and plowed-under Jerusalem.

cards.front: To what did the Sages compare the death of Gedaliah?
cards.back: To the burning of the Temple: the death of a righteous person is like the burning of the Temple. After the murder, the country was utterly desolated.

cards.front: What has the day of 10 Tevet become in the State of Israel?
cards.back: The Day of the General Kaddish: the victims of the Holocaust are remembered whose date of death is unknown.

cards.front: Which fruits are especially eaten on Tu BiShvat?
cards.back: The seven species of the Land of Israel: wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranate, olives, and dates (Devarim 8:8).

cards.front: What is a halakeh on Lag B'Omer?
cards.back: The first haircut of a three-year-old boy among many Ashkenazim. Bonfires are lit and people travel to Meron to R. Shimon bar Yochai.

cards.front: What is heard in Israel on the morning of Yom HaShoah?
cards.back: At ten in the morning a siren sounds and the country falls silent. The day is connected with the Warsaw Ghetto uprising; this is 27 Nisan.

cards.front: How is Torah studied, and when is the tallit put on, on Tisha B'Av?
cards.back: The joyful Torah is not studied: only Eichah, Iyov and the laws of mourning. The tallit and tefillin are put on not in the morning, but for Mincha.

cards.front: When will fasts like Tisha B'Av become joy?
cards.back: In the days of Mashiach, when he comes (Rambam, Laws of Fasts 5:19; Zechariah 8:19). Until he comes, the day remains mourning and hope.

questions.prompt: Why is a thirteenth month sometimes added to the Jewish calendar?
options: So that Pesach always falls in spring
So that Rosh Hashanah does not fall on Shabbat
So that the year begins in January
So that the year has exactly 365 days
questions.explanation: The lunar year is 11 days shorter than the solar one; the added Adar keeps Pesach in spring, as the Torah requires.

questions.prompt: Which month does the Torah call 'the beginning of months'?
options: Tishrei
Nisan
Elul
Adar
questions.explanation: 'This month shall be for you the beginning of months' was said of the month of the Exodus, Nisan.

questions.prompt: Which holiday lasts two days even in the Land of Israel?
options: Shavuot
Pesach (first day)
Rosh Hashanah
Yom Kippur
questions.explanation: Rosh Hashanah is celebrated for two days everywhere; Yom Kippur is one day everywhere.
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Beitzah 4b; Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 129

questions.prompt: How many days can a Jewish month have?
options: Always 30
questions.explanation: The lunar cycle is about 29.5 days, so the month lasts 29 or 30 days.

questions.prompt: Jewish days begin at midnight.
questions.explanation: Days begin at sunset: 'And there was evening, and there was morning'.

questions.prompt: The second day of a festival in the Diaspora arose because distant communities did not know exactly when the court in Jerusalem proclaimed the new month.
questions.explanation: After the calculated calendar was introduced, the custom was kept as a 'custom of the fathers'.

differs.text: Reform communities, as a rule, do not observe the second day and follow the Israeli calendar.

questions.prompt: Match the month and the holiday.
questions.explanation: The dates of the holidays are always fixed in the Jewish calendar.

questions.prompt: What is the semi-festival at the beginning of each month called (two words)?
questions.explanation: 'Head of the month' — one or two days.

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: 'Why did Chanukah fall on a different date this year than last? How does the Jewish calendar work?'
questions.modelAnswer: The Jewish calendar is lunisolar. Months begin with the new moon and last 29 or 30 days, so a regular year is about 354 days. To keep the holidays in their seasons — Pesach in spring, as Devarim 16:1 requires — a second Adar is added seven times in 19 years. That is why the dates shift on the Gregorian calendar, but in the Jewish calendar Chanukah is always 25 Kislev. Days begin in the evening, so a holiday begins the evening before, at sunset.
keyPoints: Lunar months of 29/30 days
Year ≈ 354 days
Leap Adar II, 7 times in 19 years
Pesach in spring (Devarim 16:1)
Days from evening
questions.explanation: You need to show an understanding of the lunisolar structure and its practical consequences.

questions.prompt: What is the main mitzvah of Rosh Hashanah?
options: Fasting until evening
Hearing the sound of the shofar
Living in a sukkah
Lighting eight candles
questions.explanation: The blessing is 'lishmoa kol shofar' — the mitzvah is specifically to hear the shofar.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT among the five prohibitions of Yom Kippur?
options: Wearing leather shoes
Anointing with oils
Reading books
Washing for pleasure
questions.explanation: The five prohibitions: eating and drinking, washing, anointing, leather shoes, marital relations.

questions.prompt: Where does the prayer 'Tashlich' get its name?
options: From the book of Yonah: 'and they cast Yonah into the sea'
From the book of Micah: 'And You will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea'
From the book of Tehillim: 'he who casts tears'
From Shemot: 'cast into the Nile'
questions.explanation: Tashlich means 'you shall cast'; the verse of the prophet Micah is read by a body of water.

questions.prompt: What is the concluding prayer of Yom Kippur called?
options: Musaf
Selichot
Neilah
Kol Nidrei
questions.explanation: Neilah — 'closing [of the gates]', the fifth prayer of the day, before sunset.
questions.source: Siddur, Yom Kippur; Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 133

questions.prompt: Yom Kippur atones even for sins against another person, even if one has not asked his forgiveness.
questions.explanation: Sins between a person and his fellow are atoned by Yom Kippur only if one has made peace with the one who was wronged.

questions.prompt: Match the shofar sound with its description.
questions.explanation: These are the three basic sounds of the shofar on Rosh Hashanah.
questions.source: Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 129; Siddur, Rosh Hashanah

questions.prompt: What is the name of the Aramaic formula of annulment of vows at the beginning of Yom Kippur (two words)?
questions.explanation: Kol Nidrei is recited three times before sunset.

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: 'How do you prepare for Yom Kippur, and what does teshuvah mean to you?'
questions.modelAnswer: Teshuvah is 'return': to acknowledge one's transgression, sincerely regret it, express this before the Almighty, and resolve not to repeat it. Preparation begins in Elul with the shofar and selichot, and on the Days of Awe I try to pray more and give tzedakah — 'teshuvah, tefillah and tzedakah avert the evil decree.' Before Yom Kippur I ask forgiveness from those I have hurt, for sins against other people are not atoned by Yom Kippur without this. On the eve there is the festive meal, then a 25-hour fast with the five prohibitions, Kol Nidrei in the evening and Neilah at the end.
keyPoints: Teshuvah = return; stages of repentance
Teshuvah, tefillah, tzedakah
Asking forgiveness from people (Yoma 8:9)
25-hour fast, five prohibitions
Kol Nidrei and Neilah
questions.explanation: It is important to combine knowledge of the laws with personal inner work.

questions.prompt: Explain why an apple with honey is eaten on Rosh Hashanah and what other customs there are for the festive table.
questions.modelAnswer: Rosh Hashanah is a festival, not only a day of judgment, so a festive table is laid. The apple is dipped in honey with the request 'renew for us a good and sweet year.' The challah is baked round and dipped in honey. Other simanim are eaten as well — pomegranate (so that merits may multiply), a fish head (to be a head and not a tail), dates, carrots; the set differs among Ashkenazim and Sephardim. This is not magic but a prayer expressed in action.
keyPoints: Apple with honey — a sweet year
Round challah
Simanim: pomegranate, fish head
Differences between Ashkenazim and Sephardim
questions.explanation: The customs of the festive table are symbolic wishes accompanied by prayer.

questions.prompt: Which of these species is NOT among the four species of Sukkot?
options: Myrtle
Willow
Olive branch
Etrog
questions.explanation: The four species: etrog, lulav (palm), myrtle and willow.

questions.prompt: What must s'chach — the roof of the sukkah — be like?
options: Of plant material, with more shade than light
Of transparent plastic, to see the stars
Of any material, as long as it does not leak
Of a metal lattice with branches
questions.explanation: S'chach is made of plants detached from the ground; the shade inside must be greater than the sunlight.

questions.prompt: What do the four species symbolize according to the Midrash?
options: The four directions
Four types of Jews united together
The four matriarchs
The four seasons
questions.explanation: Taste — Torah, fragrance — good deeds; different Jews bound into one bundle.

questions.prompt: What is done on Simchat Torah?
options: Fasting until midday
The annual Torah reading is completed and begun anew, dancing with the scrolls
The book of Rut is read
Beating willow branches
questions.explanation: Hakafot — seven circuits with the scrolls; the end of Devarim and the beginning of Bereshit are read.

questions.prompt: The four species are taken on all days of Sukkot, including Shabbat.
questions.explanation: On Shabbat the four species are not taken.

questions.prompt: If it rains and the food in the sukkah will be spoiled, a person is exempt from the obligation to eat in the sukkah.
questions.explanation: 'One who suffers is exempt from the sukkah.'

questions.prompt: Match the species with the plant.
questions.explanation: This is how the Oral tradition explains the verse Vayikra 23:40.

questions.prompt: What are the (Aramaic) 'guests' — the righteous who come into the sukkah — called?
questions.explanation: Avraham, Yitzchak, Yaakov, Moshe, Aharon, Yosef, David.

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: 'Why do Jews live in a sukkah for a week? What does Sukkot mean to you?'
questions.modelAnswer: The Torah commands living in the sukkah for seven days in memory of how G-d settled the people in booths in the wilderness after the Exodus (Vayikra 23:42–43). It is also the festival of the harvest ingathering and 'the time of our joy.' Leaving a solid house for a roof of branches, a person remembers that it is the Almighty who protects him, not the walls. Besides the sukkah there is the mitzvah of the four species — a symbol of the unity of different Jews. For me it is important to invite guests: the ushpizin come where guests are welcomed.
keyPoints: Memory of the wilderness (Vayikra 23:42–43)
Harvest festival, joy
Trust in G-d
Four species and unity
Hospitality, ushpizin
questions.explanation: Both the historical meaning and a personal attitude are needed.

questions.prompt: Which of these grains is NOT among the five species from which chametz can result?
options: Oats
Rye
Rice
Spelt
questions.explanation: Chametz results only from wheat, barley, spelt, rye and oats; rice belongs to kitniyot.

questions.prompt: What does tradition connect the four cups of wine at the seder with?
options: With the four matriarchs
With the four expressions of redemption in the Torah
With the four sons of the Haggadah
With the four Egyptian plagues
questions.explanation: 'I will bring out, deliver, redeem, and take' — Shemot 6:6–7.
questions.source: Shemot 6:6–7; Mishnah Pesachim 10:1; Jerusalem Talmud, Pesachim 10:1

questions.prompt: According to Rabban Gamliel, what must be explained at the seder?
options: Pesach, matzah and maror
Kiddush, karpas and charoset
The Four Questions and the four sons
The ten plagues
questions.explanation: Whoever has not explained these three things has not fulfilled the obligation.

questions.prompt: Why is the book of Rut read on Shavuot?
options: Because Ruth was born in Jerusalem
Its events take place at harvest time, and Ruth, upon entering Judaism, as it were accepted the Torah, as Israel did at Sinai
Because it describes the giving of the Torah
Because it lists the laws of Shavuot
questions.explanation: The harvest, David — a descendant of Ruth, and the parallel between Ruth's giyur and the acceptance of the Torah.

questions.prompt: On Pesach it is forbidden not only to eat chametz, but also to own it.
questions.explanation: 'Seven days shall no leaven be found in your houses.'

questions.prompt: Match the seder item with its meaning.
pairs: The bread of poverty and of the hasty Exodus
questions.explanation: The symbols of the seder plate are explained in the Haggadah.

questions.prompt: What is the story of the Exodus read at the seder called?
questions.explanation: Reading the Haggadah fulfills the mitzvah 'And you shall tell your son.'

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: 'What is close to you in the story of Ruth?'
questions.modelAnswer: Ruth was a Moabite woman who, after her husband's death, did not leave her mother-in-law Naomi and said: 'Your people shall be my people, and your G-d my G-d' (Rut 1:16). In these words are the two sides of giyur: joining the people of Israel and accepting G-d and His mitzvot. Ruth made her choice receiving nothing in return, and her great-grandson became King David. The book is read on Shavuot because the people's acceptance of the Torah at Sinai was the same decision as Ruth's. It is close to me that Judaism is faith and destiny together with the people.
keyPoints: Rut 1:16 — people and G-d
Two sides of giyur
Selfless choice
Ancestor of David (Rut 4:17)
Connection with Shavuot and Sinai
questions.explanation: A classic giyur question: it is important to show understanding of the two components of accepting Judaism.

questions.prompt: Describe how, in Orthodox practice, chametz is removed before Pesach.
questions.modelAnswer: The house is thoroughly cleaned in advance. On the night of 14 Nisan, bedikat chametz is conducted — an inspection by candlelight with the blessing 'al biur chametz'; by custom, ten pieces of bread are laid out. After the inspection, the Aramaic 'Kol Chamira' is recited — the annulment of unknown chametz. On the morning of 14 Nisan, before the end of the fifth hour, the chametz is burned (biur), and the annulment is repeated for all chametz. Chametz that one does not want to destroy is sold in advance to a non-Jew through a rabbi (mechirat chametz).
keyPoints: Bedikat chametz on the evening of the 13th / night of the 14th of Nisan
The blessing “al biur chametz”
Bitul of “Kol Chamira”
Biur on the morning of 14 Nisan
Mechirat chametz
questions.explanation: You must name all the stages in the correct order.

questions.prompt: A person completely forgot to count the Omer for an entire day. What should they do?
options: Start the count again from the first day
Stop counting until next year
Continue counting, but without the blessing
Continue with the blessing, as usual
questions.explanation: The count is continued, but the blessing is no longer said.

questions.prompt: Against which ruler did the Hasmoneans rise up?
options: Nebuchadnezzar
Antiochus IV Epiphanes
Ahasuerus
Titus
questions.explanation: Antiochus IV banned Shabbat, brit milah and the study of Torah, and defiled the Temple.

questions.prompt: How many Chanukah candles (not counting the shamash) are lit on the fifth evening of Chanukah?
options: One
Five
Four
Eight
questions.explanation: According to the school of Hillel, one candle is added each evening: on the fifth evening — five.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the four mitzvot of Purim?
options: Mishloach manot
Candle lighting
Matanot la'evyonim
Reading the Megillah
questions.explanation: The four mitzvot: the Megillah, mishloach manot, gifts to the poor, and the festive meal.

questions.prompt: In what order are the Chanukah candles lit according to the Ashkenazi custom?
options: From right to left, starting with the first candle
From left to right, starting with the newest candle
In any order
From the middle outward
questions.explanation: The candles are placed from right to left, but the first to be lit is the newest, the leftmost one.
questions.source: Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 139; Rema, Orach Chaim 676:5

questions.prompt: The name of G-d never appears in the Book of Esther.
questions.explanation: Tradition sees in this the hidden hand of the Almighty.

questions.prompt: The Chanukah lights may be used for reading.
questions.explanation: The Chanukah lights may not be used, which is why there is a shamash.

questions.prompt: What is the helper candle of the chanukiah called?
questions.explanation: The “servant” from which the other candles are lit.

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “Tell us how you will light the chanukiah on the first evening.”
questions.modelAnswer: On the evening of the first day of Chanukah, 25 Kislev, I place the chanukiah at the door, opposite the mezuzah, or in a window facing the street, to proclaim the miracle. I place one candle on the right, and the shamash. I light the shamash and recite three blessings: “lehadlik ner Chanukah,” “she'asa nissim” and — since this is the first evening — “Shehecheyanu.” Then I light the candle with the shamash. The candles must burn for at least half an hour after the stars come out; their light may not be used.
keyPoints: Location: the door or a window
One candle + the shamash
Three blessings on the first evening
Pirsumei nisa
Half an hour after the stars come out
questions.explanation: A practical question: the order of actions and the blessings matter.

questions.prompt: What happened on 9 Av, according to the Mishnah?
options: Moshe broke the tablets
The First and Second Temples were destroyed
Gedaliah was assassinated
The siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar began
questions.explanation: The 9th of Av — the decree against the generation of the desert, the destruction of both Temples, the fall of Beitar.

questions.prompt: Which event is commemorated on the Fast of 10 Tevet?
options: The beginning of the siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar
The assassination of Gedaliah
Haman's decree
The burning of the Torah by Apostomus
questions.explanation: The siege began on the tenth day of the tenth month.

questions.prompt: Why is Tu BiShvat called the New Year of the Trees?
options: The Garden of Eden was planted on this day
It is the date for calculating the age of trees and the tithe on fruit
On this day Noach planted a vineyard
The olive harvest ends on this day
questions.explanation: The Mishnah calls the 15th of Shevat the new year for trees, according to the school of Hillel.

questions.prompt: Which day of the Omer is Lag BaOmer?
options: The 18th
The 33rd
The 40th
The 49th
questions.explanation: ל״ג = 33; it is the 18th of Iyar.

questions.prompt: On minor fasts (for example, 10 Tevet), all five prohibitions of Yom Kippur apply.
questions.explanation: On minor fasts only eating and drinking are forbidden, from dawn until the stars come out.

questions.prompt: Yom HaAtzmaut is a day of thanksgiving for the proclamation of the State of Israel and for the return of the people to its Land.
questions.explanation: On 5 Iyar 5708 (May 14, 1948) the State of Israel was proclaimed. This course teaches us to mark this day as a Jewish day of joy and thanksgiving.
questions.source: Lesson: Fasts and memorial days; EJE (Electronic Jewish Encyclopedia), article “Yom HaAtzmaut”

questions.prompt: Match the fast with its date.
questions.explanation: The dates of the fasts are fixed, but when they coincide with Shabbat they are postponed.

questions.prompt: Which book of the Tanakh is read in the synagogue on the evening of Tisha B'Av?
questions.explanation: Eichah — the Lamentations of Yirmiyahu over the destruction of Jerusalem.

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “Why fast on Tisha B'Av today, when there is a State of Israel?”
questions.modelAnswer: Tisha B'Av is the memory of the destruction of both Temples and of the other catastrophes that happened on this day (Mishnah Taanit 4:6). The Talmud teaches that the Second Temple was destroyed because of baseless hatred, so this day is a time to reflect on the unity of the people and on relationships between people. The Temple has not been rebuilt, and tradition sees in the fast an expression of hope for complete redemption; the prophet Zecharyah promised that the fasts will become days of joy. I know that the positions differ: Conservative (Masorti) Judaism keeps the fast, sometimes changing the wording of the prayers, while in Reform communities it is above all a day of remembrance.
keyPoints: The destruction of both Temples (Taanit 4:6)
Baseless hatred (Yoma 9b)
Hope for redemption (Zecharyah 8:19)
Respect for different positions
questions.explanation: A good answer combines the historical meaning, the moral lesson, and knowledge of the positions of the movements.

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “How do you know when a holiday begins and ends, and how many days do you observe it?”
questions.modelAnswer: I look at the Jewish calendar: it gives the candle-lighting time and the time when the holiday ends. The day begins at sunset, so if Pesach falls on Wednesday, the first seder will be on Tuesday evening, and the day ends with the appearance of the stars. Twilight, bein ha-shmashot, is a doubtful time, so the holiday is accepted early and ended with a margin. The second day in the Diaspora was kept as a custom of our fathers even after the calculated calendar came into being; Rosh Hashanah lasts two days everywhere, and Yom Kippur — one. How many days of Pesach, Shavuot and Sukkot to observe, I will take from the custom of my community and confirm with the rabbi.
keyPoints: The calendar gives candle-lighting time and the end of the holiday
The day begins at sunset, the end comes with the stars
Bein ha-shmashot: begin early, end late
Second day — a custom of our fathers; Rosh Hashanah two days, Yom Kippur one
questions.explanation: The beit din checks whether a person can determine the boundaries of a holiday on their own and knows how many days are customary in their community.

differs.text: Reform communities usually observe the holidays according to the calendar of Eretz Israel: seven days of Pesach, one day of Shavuot, and in many communities — one day of Rosh Hashanah.

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “How will you spend Rosh Hashanah, and why do we hear the shofar on this day?”
questions.modelAnswer: Rosh Hashanah is for me both a festival and a day of judgment: the Almighty judges the world, and in prayer I accept Him as King. I will come to the synagogue to fulfill the principal mitzvah — to hear the shofar: the blessing says “to hear the voice of the shofar.” Tekiah is a long blast, shevarim — three groans, teruah — short, staccato sounds; the Rambam wrote that the shofar is like a call to wake up, remember the Creator and return. In the evening there will be a festive table: a round challah and an apple with honey, asking for a good and sweet year, and in the afternoon of the first day — tashlich by the water. In Musaf I want to hear the three themes: Malchuyot, Zichronot and Shofarot. If the first day falls on Shabbat, in traditional practice the shofar is not blown that day, and it is heard on the second day.
keyPoints: The day of judgment and accepting the kingship of the Almighty
The mitzvah — to hear the shofar
Tekiah, shevarim and teruah
Festive meal, tashlich, and the three themes of Musaf
questions.explanation: The beit din listens for whether a person distinguishes the mitzvah of the shofar from table customs and how they will spend the day.

differs.text: In many Reform communities Rosh Hashanah is celebrated for one day, and if it falls on Shabbat, the shofar is blown even on Shabbat.

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “How will you mark Sukkot: what will you do in the sukkah and with the four species?”
questions.modelAnswer: On Sukkot I will try to eat in the sukkah: the Torah commands us to live in booths for seven days in memory of how the Almighty housed the people in booths in the desert. Before eating one says “leishev ba'sukkah.” S'chach is made of plants that grew from the ground and were detached from it, and there must be more shade inside than sunlight: this is how I remember that it is not the house that guards me, but the Almighty. The four species — the etrog, the lulav, three myrtle branches and two willow branches — I will take with the blessing and wave them in six directions; on Shabbat they are not taken. On Simchat Torah I will come to the hakafot: the reading of Devarim is completed and Bereshit is begun at once; in Israel this is the day of Shemini Atzeret, in the Diaspora — the following day.
keyPoints: Eating in the sukkah and the blessing “leishev ba'sukkah”
S'chach from plants, more shade than sunlight
The four species and waving them in six directions, except on Shabbat
Simchat Torah: end of Devarim, beginning of Bereshit, hakafot
questions.explanation: The beit din checks whether a person connects the mitzvah of the sukkah and the four species with what they will actually do.

differs.text: In Reform communities of the Diaspora, Simchat Torah is celebrated on Shemini Atzeret, as in Israel, and women and men take part as equals.

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “What will you do at the seder, and what does it mean for you to see yourself as having gone out of Egypt?”
questions.modelAnswer: On the first evening of Pesach I will hold the seder and read the Haggadah: this is the mitzvah of telling the story of the Exodus. I will drink four cups of wine or grape juice — “I will bring out,” “I will deliver,” “I will redeem,” “I will take” — leaning to the left side, like a free person. At the table I will explain the three things without which, in the words of Rabban Gamliel, the obligation is not fulfilled: the Pesach sacrifice, the matzah and the maror. Matzah is the bread of poverty and of the hasty departure; maror is the bitterness of slavery. For me, the words of the Mishnah that in every generation a person must see themselves as having gone out of Egypt mean: this freedom is mine, and from Pesach I go on to the responsibility that the Torah gives at Shavuot. If my community keeps two festival days, there will be a seder on the second evening as well.
keyPoints: The Haggadah — the story of the Exodus
Four cups and the four words of redemption
Pesach, matzah and maror
Seeing oneself as having left Egypt and moving on to Shavuot
questions.explanation: The beit din wants to hear a living seder: the freedom of the Exodus must become personal, not only a ban on chametz.

differs.text: Reform communities usually keep Pesach according to the calendar of Eretz Israel: a seder on the first evening, not on the first two, as in the traditional Diaspora.

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “How will you mark Purim? Which mitzvot will you fulfill on this day?”
questions.modelAnswer: I greet Purim, 14 Adar, as the day of deliverance from Haman's decree: the date was chosen by lot, pur, and in the Book of Esther the name of G-d is not mentioned — the Almighty acts in hidden ways. In the evening and in the morning I will hear the Megillah in full, every word, with the blessing “al mikra megillah.” By day I will send at least two kinds of ready-made food to at least one person and give gifts to at least two poor people. The Sages taught that it is better to spend more on the poor than on the feast and on gifts to friends, and I want to do just that. During the day I will sit down to the seudat Purim, and on the eve, 13 Adar, I will try to keep the Fast of Esther.
keyPoints: The Megillah in the evening and in the morning, every word
Mishloach manot: two kinds of food to one person
Matanot la'evyonim to two poor people, without stinting
The daytime meal and the Fast of Esther on the eve
questions.explanation: The beit din checks the four mitzvot of Purim and whether a person puts helping the poor side by side with the joy of the table.

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “How will you keep the fasts, and how will you mark Yom HaShoah and Yom HaAtzmaut?”
questions.modelAnswer: For me a fast is the memory of catastrophe and a time to look back at one's deeds: the Rambam writes that it awakens the heart to repentance, and the main thing is the inner change. The great fast, Tisha B'Av, lasts from sunset until the stars come out the next day and includes five prohibitions; Eichah is read in the evening — I will come to hear it, and I will fast in the way customary in my community. The minor fasts — 17 Tammuz, the Fast of Gedaliah, 10 Tevet and the Fast of Esther — run from dawn until the stars come out, and in them only eating and drinking are forbidden. Tisha B'Av is for me also the grief over the exile from the Land and the hope for a rebuilt Temple. Yom HaShoah, 27 Nisan, I will mark as a day of remembrance of the Holocaust and of heroism. Yom HaAtzmaut is a day of thanksgiving for the State of Israel and for the return of the people to its Land; Yom Yerushalayim — for the reunified Jerusalem, the eternal capital. How exactly my community prays on these days, I will clarify with the rabbi, but the attitude toward these days itself is, for me, part of the Jewish path.
keyPoints: A fast — remembrance and teshuvah, not an end in itself
The great fast: sunset to the stars, five prohibitions
A minor fast: from dawn, only food and drink
Tisha B'Av — grief over the exile and hope for the Temple
Yom HaShoah — remembrance; Yom HaAtzmaut and Yom Yerushalayim — thanksgiving for the Land and Israel
questions.explanation: The beit din looks at whether a person distinguishes the kinds of fasts and speaks of Eretz Israel and the State with clarity and respect.

differs.text: In many Reform communities Tisha B'Av is a day of remembrance with the reading of Eichah, while the fast itself is a matter of personal choice.

questions.prompt: On which date of the Jewish calendar does Chanukah always fall?
options: On 25 Kislev
On 15 Nisan
On 10 Tishrei
On 6 Sivan
questions.explanation: In the Jewish calendar the dates of the holidays are fixed: Chanukah is always on 25 Kislev, although on the Gregorian calendar it shifts.

questions.prompt: Which mitzvah did the people receive first, already in Egypt, on the eve of the Exodus?
options: To eat matzah on the night of the Exodus from Egypt
To sanctify the arrival of the new month
To live in booths during the forty years in the desert
To blow the shofar in the seventh month
questions.explanation: The lesson calls the sanctification of the month the people's first mitzvah in Egypt: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months” (Shemot 12:2).

questions.prompt: From which month does the Torah count the months, and when does the year number change?
options: Months from Tishrei, and the year number from 1 Nisan
Months from Elul, and the year number from 15 Shevat
Months from Nisan, and the year number from 1 Tishrei
Months from Adar, and the year number from 1 Elul
questions.explanation: The months are counted from Nisan, the month of the Exodus, and the year number changes on Rosh Hashanah, 1 Tishrei. These are two different reckonings of one and the same calendar.

questions.prompt: Whom does tradition name as the publisher of the fixed calculated calendar?
options: Rabbi Akiva, around 135 CE
Hillel the Elder, in the time of the Temple
The Rambam, in the twelfth century
The patriarch Hillel II, around 359 CE
questions.explanation: When testimony about the new moon became impossible, the fixed calendar was published — by tradition — by the patriarch Hillel II around 359 CE.

questions.prompt: What is the “half” Hallel on Rosh Chodesh?
options: Psalms 113–118, but with omissions
Psalms 113–118 in full, without omissions
Only one psalm, the 150th
Psalms 120–134, the Songs of Ascents
questions.explanation: On Rosh Chodesh the half Hallel is read: the psalms of praise 113–118, but not all the verses — with omissions.

questions.prompt: The familiar names of the months — Nisan, Tishrei, Adar — came from the Babylonian exile.
questions.explanation: The lesson says that the Jews brought the names of the months from the Babylonian exile, while in the Torah itself the months are more often called by number.

questions.prompt: One who forgot “Yaaleh Veyavo” in the evening Amidah of Rosh Chodesh must repeat the Amidah.
questions.explanation: In the evening the Amidah is not repeated: in the time of the Sanhedrin the month was not sanctified at night. It is repeated if the insertion was forgotten in the morning or during the day.
questions.source: Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 97; Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 422:1

questions.prompt: Match the date of each “new year” from the Mishnah with what it was established for.
questions.explanation: The Mishnah has four new years: Nisan — for kings and festivals; Elul — for cattle; Tishrei — for years and for shemitah and yovel; 15 Shevat — for trees.

questions.prompt: What is the leap, “pregnant” year called in Hebrew? Two words.
questions.explanation: The lesson calls a year with an added second Adar shanah me'uberet, literally a “pregnant year.”

questions.prompt: At the interview you are asked: “How do you mark Rosh Chodesh — the home semi-festival and the prayer in the synagogue?”
questions.modelAnswer: Rosh Chodesh is for me a minor festival at the beginning of the month. If the previous month lasted thirty days, two days are observed — the thirtieth and the first; if twenty-nine — only the first. In prayer, “Yaaleh Veyavo” is inserted, the half Hallel is read, a passage of Torah and Musaf. On the Shabbat before it, the day of the new moon is announced in the synagogue and it is blessed. I also remember the women's custom of easing heavy work: according to the midrash, the women did not hand over their ornaments for the golden calf.
keyPoints: One day or two, depending on the length of the previous month
Yaaleh Veyavo, half Hallel, Torah portion, Musaf
Blessing the month on the preceding Shabbat
The women's custom and the midrash about the calf
questions.explanation: The lesson describes Rosh Chodesh as a semi-festival with special insertions in the prayers and a custom for women.

questions.prompt: A question from the beit din: “Name the leap years of the nineteen-year cycle and say when Purim falls in such a year.”
questions.modelAnswer: The lunar year is shorter than the solar year, and without the adjustment Pesach would drift away from spring, while the Torah commands us to keep the month of Aviv. In the nineteen-year cycle a second Adar is added seven times: in years 3, 6, 8, 11, 14, 17 and 19. Such a year is called shanah me'uberet. Purim is then celebrated not in the first Adar but in the second, closer to Pesach. This is how the festival of freedom remains a spring one.
keyPoints: Seven years of the cycle: 3, 6, 8, 11, 14, 17 and 19
A second Adar is added
Purim in Adar Bet
The goal — to keep Pesach in spring
questions.explanation: The lesson lists the seven leap years of the cycle and says that in such a year Purim is celebrated in the second Adar.

questions.prompt: What is the Shabbat between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur called?
options: Shabbat HaGadol before Pesach
Shabbat Shuvah
The Shabbat on which the month is blessed
The Shabbat before the fast of 9 Av
questions.explanation: The lesson calls the Shabbat between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur outright Shabbat Shuvah, the Shabbat of return.
questions.source: Lesson: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur: The Days of Awe

questions.prompt: How many communal prayers are recited on Yom Kippur?
options: Three: evening, morning and additional
Four: without a separate afternoon service
Five: Maariv, Shacharit, Musaf, Mincha and Ne'ilah
Six: Ne'ilah is recited twice
questions.explanation: On Yom Kippur one prays five times: Maariv, Shacharit, Musaf, Mincha, and the final Ne'ilah, the “closing of the gates.”
questions.source: Lesson: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur: The Days of Awe

questions.prompt: How many shofar blasts are sounded by custom during the morning of Rosh Hashanah?
options: Thirty blasts in the morning
Forty blasts in the morning
Fifty blasts in the morning
One hundred blasts in the morning
questions.explanation: The lesson says: by custom, one hundred blasts are sounded in the synagogue on the morning of Rosh Hashanah.
questions.source: Lesson: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur: The Days of Awe

questions.prompt: How many times is “The L-rd, He is G-d” said at the end of Ne'ilah?
options: Seven times
Once, like the Shema
Three times, like “Baruch Shem”
Ten times, for the ten days of teshuvah
questions.explanation: At the end of Ne'ilah the Shema is said once, “Baruch Shem…” three times, and “The L-rd, He is G-d” seven times; then the shofar is sounded.
questions.source: Lesson: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur: The Days of Awe

questions.prompt: In the month of Elul the shofar is blown in the synagogue each morning in preparation for the Days of Awe.
questions.explanation: Preparation for the Days of Awe begins a month in advance: in Elul the shofar is blown in the synagogue each morning (by Ashkenazi custom; it is not blown on Shabbat or on the eve of Rosh Hashanah).
questions.source: Lesson: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur: The Days of Awe

questions.prompt: Selichot are read from the end of Elul, and among Sephardim — from the very beginning of Elul.
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes the customs in exactly this way: Ashkenazim read Selichot from the end of Elul, Sephardim — from the beginning of the month.
questions.source: Lesson: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur: The Days of Awe

questions.prompt: Kol Nidrei cancels agreements and promises made to other people.
questions.explanation: Kol Nidrei releases a person's vows to G-d. This formula does not cancel promises and agreements made with other people.
questions.source: Lesson: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur: The Days of Awe

questions.prompt: Match the three themes of the Rosh Hashanah Musaf with their meanings.
pairs: Remembrance of creation and of the covenant
The shofar of Sinai and of the future redemption
questions.explanation: The Musaf of Rosh Hashanah is built on three themes: the kingship of the Almighty, remembrance, and the shofar — at Sinai and in the future redemption.
questions.source: Lesson: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur: The Days of Awe

questions.prompt: What is the last meal before the Yom Kippur fast called? Two words.
questions.explanation: On the eve of Yom Kippur there is a mitzvah to eat well; the last meal before the fast is called seudah mafseket.
questions.source: Lesson: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur: The Days of Awe

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “What are kapparot, what other custom of the eve of Yom Kippur do you know, and was there a controversy about these customs?”
questions.modelAnswer: For me, kapparot is a custom of the eve, not a mitzvah of the Torah. A chicken is swung over the head, or — as is more common now — money, and then it is given to the poor. I know that the Rashba and Rabbi Yosef Karo were opposed, while the Rema supported the custom, so I will ask the rabbi what is accepted among us. On this eve, men customarily immerse in the mikveh. For me, the fast itself and asking people for forgiveness matter more than the rite.
keyPoints: Kapparot: a chicken or money, then to the poor
Controversy: Rashba and Karo against, Rema for
Men's immersion in the mikveh
A custom of the eve, not a mitzvah of the Torah
questions.explanation: The lesson places kapparot and the mikveh on the eve of Yom Kippur and conveys the controversy among the medieval authorities.
questions.source: Lesson: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur: The Days of Awe

questions.prompt: What is Sukkot called in the festival prayers?
options: Zman heruteinu, the time of our freedom
Zman simchateinu, the time of our joy
Zman matan Torateinu, the time of the giving of the Torah
Shabbat shabbaton, the Sabbath of Sabbaths
questions.explanation: The Torah calls us to rejoice in the festival, so in the prayers Sukkot is zman simchateinu, “the time of our joy.”

questions.prompt: How many days after Yom Kippur does Sukkot begin?
options: The next day, 11 Tishrei
Three days later, 13 Tishrei
Five days later, 15 Tishrei
Ten days later, 20 Tishrei
questions.explanation: Sukkot begins on 15 Tishrei, five days after Yom Kippur.
questions.source: Lesson: Sukkot, Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah

questions.prompt: Where do the righteous guests come, according to the tradition of the ushpizin?
options: If the sukkah stands only on the east side of the courtyard
If the host reads the Zohar aloud all night
If all four species lie on the table
If living guests are welcomed, especially the poor
questions.explanation: The righteous guests come where earthly guests are also welcomed, especially the poor: without hospitality, the ushpizin do not come.
questions.source: Lesson: Sukkot, Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah

questions.prompt: What is the minimum number of walls a sukkah must have?
options: Three: two full walls and one partial wall suffice
Two solid walls strictly facing each other
Four blank walls with no opening
One wall and posts at the corners
questions.explanation: By halacha there are no fewer than three walls; two full walls and a third partial one are permitted.

questions.prompt: A sukkah may be set up under a spreading tree if the s'chach is made correctly.
questions.explanation: A sukkah is set up under the open sky, not under a tree or a balcony: there must be no other roof above the s'chach.
questions.source: Lesson: Sukkot, Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah

questions.prompt: In the Diaspora, Simchat Torah falls on the same day as Shemini Atzeret.
questions.explanation: In Eretz Israel, Simchat Torah coincides with Shemini Atzeret; in the Diaspora it is the following day, 23 Tishrei.
questions.source: Lesson: Sukkot, Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah

differs.text: In Reform communities of the Diaspora, Simchat Torah is celebrated on Shemini Atzeret, according to the calendar of Eretz Israel, and not as a separate following day.

questions.prompt: Match each of the four species with what it has.
questions.explanation: This is how the lesson breaks down the four species: the etrog has taste and scent, the date has taste, the myrtle has scent, and the willow has neither.

questions.prompt: What are the weekdays within the festival called, when some work is already permitted?
questions.explanation: After yom tov come the days of Chol HaMoed, “the intermediate days of the festival”: some work is permitted, but the festive atmosphere remains.
questions.source: Lesson: Sukkot, Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah

questions.prompt: What is the memorial prayer that Ashkenazim recite on Shemini Atzeret called?
questions.explanation: Ashkenazim recite the memorial prayer Yizkor on Shemini Atzeret; on the same day they begin the prayer for rain.
questions.source: Lesson: Sukkot, Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “What happens on Simchat Torah, and why is the Torah reading begun again right away?”
questions.modelAnswer: On Simchat Torah, the annual cycle of reading is concluded with the last parashah of the book of Devarim and begun again at once from the first parashah of Bereshit: the Torah has no end, it is studied always. All the scrolls are taken out of the ark, and the community dances around the bimah with them seven times — these are the hakafot. The one called up to the last passage is called Chatan Torah, and the one called to the first — Chatan Bereshit. In Israel this festival coincides with Shemini Atzeret; in the Diaspora it is the following day, 23 Tishrei. In an Orthodox community, men are called up to the Torah, and women celebrate from their side of the synagogue.
keyPoints: The end of Devarim and at once the beginning of Bereshit: the Torah has no end
Hakafot — seven circuits with the scrolls
Chatan Torah and Chatan Bereshit
In Israel together with Shemini Atzeret, in the Diaspora on 23 Tishrei
questions.explanation: The lesson describes Simchat Torah: the completion and new beginning of the reading, the hakafot, the honorary call-ups, and the difference between Israel and the Diaspora.
questions.source: Lesson: Sukkot, Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah

differs.text: In egalitarian Masorti communities, women are also called up to the Torah; the roles of “kallat Torah” and “kallat Bereshit” are performed by women.
In Reform communities of the Diaspora, Simchat Torah is celebrated on Shemini Atzeret, as in Israel; men and women take part on equal terms, and children beginning their studies are often honored.

questions.prompt: A question from the beit din: “What is special about Hoshana Rabbah, and why is Shemini Atzeret already a different festival?”
questions.modelAnswer: For me, Hoshana Rabbah is the seventh day of Sukkot, 21 Tishrei, not an ordinary weekday of the festival. Seven circuits are made with the four species, and then a bundle of willows is beaten on the ground. According to tradition, the verdict of the Days of Awe is finally sealed here, so on the preceding night many stay up studying. The next day, 22 Tishrei, Shemini Atzeret is already a separate festival: the Almighty, as it were, asks us to stay one more day. In Musaf they begin Geshem, and Ashkenazim recite Yizkor.
keyPoints: 21 Tishrei: seven circuits and the beating of the willows
The verdict is sealed, the night in study
22 Tishrei — a separate Shemini Atzeret
Geshem and the Ashkenazi Yizkor
questions.explanation: The lesson separates Hoshana Rabbah within Sukkot from Shemini Atzeret and connects this day with the prayer for rain.

questions.prompt: What does the prayer name of Pesach, “zman heruteinu,” mean?
options: The time of our joy, the festival of huts
The time of our freedom, remembrance of the Exodus
The time of the giving of the Torah at Mount Sinai
The Sabbath of Sabbaths and the day of the strict fast
questions.explanation: Pesach is the festival of the Exodus, and in the prayers it is called zman heruteinu, “the time of our freedom.”
questions.source: Lesson: Pesach, the Counting of the Omer and Shavuot

questions.prompt: Why are weddings not held and haircuts not given during the days of the Omer count?
options: It is a fast in memory of the destruction of both Temples
This is how the wheat harvest is welcomed at Mount Sinai
In memory of Rabbi Akiva's students, who died at that time
Until Shavuot, any joy of freedom is forbidden
questions.explanation: The days of the Omer are a semi-mourning in memory of the students of Rabbi Akiva (Yevamot 62b): weddings are not held and hair is not cut.

questions.prompt: Within what time must the matzah dough reach the oven so as not to become chametz?
options: No more than forty minutes after kneading
No more than an hour from rolling out to the oven
No more than nine minutes over a strong flame
No more than eighteen minutes from the water to the baking
questions.explanation: Matzah is baked from the same grains and water, but no more than eighteen minutes may pass from the mixing to the baking.
questions.source: Lesson: Pesach, the Counting of the Omer and Shavuot

questions.prompt: A person forgot the Omer count in the evening and remembered only during the day. How should they count from then on?
options: During the day without the blessing, and in the evenings that follow — with it
They skip that day and continue with the blessing
They stop counting until the end of the season
That day, and afterwards they count only without the blessing
questions.explanation: One who forgot in the evening counts during the day without the blessing, and from the following evenings — again with the blessing. A different rule applies if an entire day has been missed.

questions.prompt: At the seder, the four cups are drunk reclining on the left side.
questions.explanation: The four cups are drunk reclining on the left, as free people did at a meal.

questions.prompt: On Pesach, Ashkenazim and Sephardim alike eat rice, legumes and corn.
questions.explanation: These are kitniyot: by custom Ashkenazim do not eat them, while Sephardim do. The two traditions have no single practice in common.
questions.source: Lesson: Pesach, the Counting of the Omer and Shavuot

differs.text: In 2015, the Committee on Jewish Law and Standards of the Conservative movement permitted Ashkenazim to eat kitniyot, although many families keep the former custom.

questions.prompt: Match the seder step with what is done at it.
pairs: Bitter herbs with matzah, the custom of Hillel
The blessing after the meal, the third cup
questions.explanation: The lesson lists the fifteen steps of the seder from the beginning; among them are kiddush, karpas, Hillel's korech, the blessing after the meal and the afikoman.

questions.prompt: What is the nighttime Torah study of the Shavuot festival called?
questions.explanation: Many stay awake on the night of Shavuot and study Torah: this is Tikkun Leil Shavuot.
questions.source: Lesson: Pesach, the Counting of the Omer and Shavuot

questions.prompt: At the interview you are asked: “What do chametz and matzah say about a person, not only about the kitchen?”
questions.modelAnswer: When I remove chametz, I think about more than dishes. Leavened dough that has risen and puffed up is, for me, an image of arrogance. Matzah from the same grain is simplicity and humility: the dough was not allowed to rise. The Torah forbids chametz both to be eaten and to be kept in the house, and I take this seriously. I eat matzah as the bread of poverty and a sign of the hasty Exodus.
keyPoints: Chametz — an image of arrogance
Matzah — simplicity and humility
Chametz may be neither eaten nor kept
Matzah — the bread of poverty and haste
questions.explanation: The lesson directly compares chametz with arrogance and “puffed-up” self-importance, and matzah with simplicity and humility.

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “In what way was Shavuot a harvest festival, and in what way has it become the day of the Torah? How will you spend the night?”
questions.modelAnswer: Shavuot is 6 Sivan, the fiftieth day of the count; in the Diaspora I remember that the festival lasts two days. In the Torah it is the wheat harvest and the first fruits, bikkurim. Tradition sees here above all the giving of the Torah at Sinai, and in the synagogue the Ten Commandments are read. I want to spend the night in study, decorate the home with greenery and set a dairy table. On this day the Book of Ruth is read: for me, its “your people shall be my people” and the acceptance of the Torah at Sinai are one and the same decision.
keyPoints: 6 Sivan, the fiftieth day; in the Diaspora two days
In the Torah it is the harvest and bikkurim, in tradition — the giving of the Torah
The Ten Commandments, nighttime study, greenery, dairy foods
The Book of Ruth and the acceptance of the Torah
questions.explanation: The lesson combines the agricultural meaning of Shavuot, the giving of the Torah, and the customs of the night, the table and the reading of Ruth.

questions.prompt: What does the name of the festival “Chanukah” mean?
options: “Concealment,” as hinted in the name Esther
“Dedication,” the renewal of the Temple
“The miracle of the oil” from the jug that was found
“Victory” of the army over King Antiochus
questions.explanation: The Temple was consecrated anew on 25 Kislev, and the word “Chanukah” itself the lesson translates as “dedication, renewal.”

questions.prompt: On which day of Adar is Purim celebrated in most cities?
options: 13 Adar, on the fast day itself
15 Adar, together with the capital Shushan
14 Adar, the day after the rescue
16 Adar, after two days of feasting
questions.explanation: Purim is celebrated on 14 Adar. 15 Adar, Shushan Purim, is observed in cities that were walled in the days of Yehoshua, above all in Jerusalem.

questions.prompt: From what trouble did Chanukah save the people, according to the lesson — in contrast to Purim?
options: From famine in besieged Jerusalem
From a decree to destroy everyone in a single day
From a ban on building sukkot in exile
From spiritual destruction and the desecration of the Temple
questions.explanation: Both festivals are about rescue: Chanukah — from spiritual destruction, Purim — from physical destruction.

questions.prompt: On the Friday of Chanukah, when is the chanukiah lit in relation to the Shabbat candles?
options: Before the Shabbat candles, and the candles are made longer
Right after the Shabbat candles, with the same flame
Only after havdalah, when Shabbat has departed
At midday on Friday, together with Minchah
questions.explanation: On Friday the chanukiah is lit before the Shabbat candles, and larger candles are used. At the close of Shabbat, at home it is lit after havdalah.

questions.prompt: How long must the Chanukah lights burn after the stars appear?
options: At least ten minutes
At least half an hour
At least two hours
Until dawn itself, without interruption
questions.explanation: The lesson sets the duration: the lights burn at least half an hour after the stars come out.

questions.prompt: Chanukah and Purim are commanded in the Five Books of Moshe, so work is forbidden on these days, as on Shabbat.
questions.explanation: Chanukah and Purim are not mentioned in the Five Books of Moshe: the Sages and the prophets instituted them in memory of later miracles. Work is not forbidden on these days, but there are special mitzvot and the insert “Al HaNissim.”

questions.prompt: Drinking on Purim to the point of intoxication that harms a person is the fulfillment of a mitzvah.
questions.explanation: The Talmud says to drink until one cannot tell apart “cursed is Haman” and “blessed is Mordechai,” but the Rema explains: a little more than usual is enough, until one dozes off. Dangerous drunkenness is not a mitzvah.

questions.prompt: Match the letter on the sevivon outside Israel with the word from the phrase “Nes gadol haya sham.”
questions.explanation: On the dreidel outside Israel the letters are nun, gimel, hei and shin: “Nes gadol haya sham,” “A great miracle happened there.”

questions.prompt: What is the money that is customary to give children on Chanukah called?
questions.explanation: Among the customs of Chanukah, the lesson names the gift to children — Chanukah gelt.

questions.prompt: Explain to a child why Chanukah lasts eight days and what the jug of oil has to do with it.
questions.modelAnswer: I will tell the child that the Hasmoneans cleansed the Temple and consecrated it again on 25 Kislev: that is where the name Chanukah comes from. They found one jug of pure oil bearing the seal of the High Priest, enough for one day. The lamp burned for eight days while new oil was being prepared — so the Talmud tells it. The following year they made these days a festival of praise and thanksgiving. That is why each evening the number of lights grows by one, up to eight.
keyPoints: The consecration of the Temple on 25 Kislev
One jug lasted eight days
The festival was instituted the following year
The lights are added up to eight
questions.explanation: The lesson conveys the miracle of the oil and the eight days of the festival according to the Talmud, Shabbat 21b.

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “How will you hear the Megillah on Purim, and who may read it for the community?”
questions.modelAnswer: The Megillah, the Book of Esther, is heard twice: in the evening and in the morning. The reader says the blessing “al mikra megillah,” and I must hear every word, so the noise of the graggers at the name of Haman must not keep me from hearing the text. Women are also obligated to hear the Megillah. In an Orthodox community a man usually reads for everyone; whether a woman may read for men is a matter of controversy, but there are women's readings for women.
keyPoints: Twice: in the evening and in the morning
The blessing “al mikra megillah,” hearing every word
Noise at the name of Haman
Women are obligated; reading for men — a controversy
questions.explanation: The lesson describes the reading of the Megillah as the first mitzvah of Purim and the difference in who reads it for the community.

differs.text: In Conservative communities, women read the Megillah for the whole community and count as fulfilling the mitzvah for others, just as men do.

questions.prompt: How long do the minor fasts last, such as 17 Tammuz and 10 Tevet?
options: From sunset the day before to sunset of the fast day
From midnight to noon of the following day
From dawn until the stars come out on that same day
From noon to midnight without interruption
questions.explanation: The minor fasts last from dawn until the stars come out, and on them only eating and drinking are forbidden.

questions.prompt: What happens in Israel at ten in the morning on Yom HaShoah?
options: In synagogues the festive Hallel is recited
A minor fast is declared until the stars come out
Bonfires are lit, as on Lag BaOmer
A siren sounds, and the whole country stands still
questions.explanation: Yom HaShoah is 27 Nisan. At ten in the morning a siren sounds in Israel, and the whole country stands still.

questions.prompt: When is Yom Yerushalayim observed, and what is remembered?
options: 28 Iyar — the reunification of Jerusalem, the eternal capital, in 1967
27 Nisan — remembrance of the Shoah and the Warsaw uprising
5 Iyar — the proclamation of the State in 1948
15 Shevat — the New Year for trees according to the Mishnah
questions.explanation: Yom Yerushalayim is 28 Iyar, the day of the reunification of Jerusalem in 1967. Jerusalem is the eternal and undivided capital of the Jewish people.

questions.prompt: If the fast of 17 Tammuz falls on Shabbat, to which day is it postponed?
options: To the preceding Thursday
To the nearest Sunday
It is not postponed: people fast on Shabbat
To 10 Tevet of the same year
questions.explanation: If a fast falls on Shabbat, 17 Tammuz, 9 Av and the Fast of Gedaliah are postponed to Sunday. The Fast of Esther is postponed to Thursday.

questions.prompt: The prophet Zechariah says that in the future the four fasts will become days of joy.
questions.explanation: Zechariah promises: the fasts of the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth months will become days of joy and gladness.

questions.prompt: According to the current calendar, the fast of 10 Tevet sometimes falls on Shabbat.
questions.explanation: The lesson says that in our calendar 10 Tevet never falls on Shabbat. Other fasts, when they coincide with Shabbat, are postponed.

questions.prompt: Among Ashkenazim, during the “Nine Days” from 1 Av, meat is not eaten and wine is not drunk, except on Shabbat.
questions.explanation: From 1 Av the “Nine Days” apply among Ashkenazim: meat and wine are set aside, except on Shabbat. Among Sephardim some of the restrictions apply only in the week of the fast itself.

questions.prompt: Match the name with the event remembered on a fast or on Tisha B'Av.
pairs: The governor of Judea after the First Temple
Killed Gedaliah, and the people fled to Egypt
Burned a Torah scroll on 17 Tammuz
Began the siege of Jerusalem on 10 Tevet
questions.explanation: The lesson connects these names with the Fast of Gedaliah, the five calamities of 17 Tammuz, the fall of Betar and the beginning of the Babylonian siege.

questions.prompt: What are the “Three Weeks” of mourning from 17 Tammuz to 9 Av called in Hebrew?
questions.explanation: The period from 17 Tammuz to 9 Av the lesson calls Bein HaMetzarim — the “Three Weeks” of mourning.

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “How does the evening of 9 Av pass in the synagogue, and what restrictions of the major fast do you take upon yourself?”
questions.modelAnswer: I observe Tisha B'Av as a major fast: from sunset to the appearance of the stars, without food and drink, washing for pleasure, anointing, leather shoes, or intimacy. In the evening I sit on low seats in dim light and listen to Eicha, and in the morning — kinot. I do not study joyful Torah on this day, I avoid greetings, and I put on tallit and tefillin for Minchah, not in the morning. It matters to me to remember: the Second Temple fell because of causeless hatred, so the fast tests my relations with people as well. Zechariah promised that this day, too, will yet become joy.
keyPoints: A major fast of nearly a full day and five restrictions
Eicha in the evening on low seats, kinot in the morning
No joyful Torah; tallit and tefillin for Minchah
Causeless hatred and Zechariah's promise
questions.explanation: The lesson describes Tisha B'Av as a major fast with the reading of Eicha and adds restrictions on study, greetings, and the time of tefillin.
questions.source: Mishnah Taanit 4:6; Eicha 1:1; Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 124

questions.prompt: With what hope do we mourn the Temples on Tisha B'Av?
options: Mashiach has already come, so the Temple is no longer needed
The fasts have already become festivals because the State of Israel exists
The Temples will be rebuilt when Mashiach comes, whom we still await
Mourning was cancelled forever after the destruction of the Second Temple
questions.explanation: Tisha B'Av joins mourning for the Temples with the hope that they will be rebuilt when Mashiach comes, whom we still await.
questions.source: Rambam, Laws of Kings 11:1, 11:4; Laws of Fasts 5:19

questions.prompt: When Mashiach comes, Tisha B'Av will remain a day of mourning forever.
questions.explanation: Rambam writes that in the days of Mashiach these fasts will become days of joy and festival. As long as he has not come, Tisha B'Av remains mourning and hope.

questions.prompt: Which prophet said: “instead of bulls, the words of our lips”?
options: Hoshea 14:3
Yeshayahu 2:4
Yirmiyahu 23:5
Zechariah 9:9
questions.explanation: “Instead of bulls, the words of our lips”: teshuvah and prayer open the way to forgiveness.

questions.prompt: How do many Reform communities in the Diaspora observe the length of festivals such as Pesach or Shemini Atzeret / Simchat Torah?
options: By the Israeli calendar: without the second day of the Diaspora, and Simchat Torah is combined with Shemini Atzeret
Always one day longer than in Israel, and never otherwise
The festivals are moved to the nearest Sunday
They celebrate only the days that coincide with civil weekends
questions.explanation: Many progressive communities in the Diaspora keep the Israeli length of the festival; check the custom of your synagogue.
questions.source: Lessons on the calendar and on Sukkot / Simchat Torah

questions.prompt: How do many Reform communities relate to Tisha B'Av today?
options: They often mark it with the reading of Eicha and reflection on the destructions and the sorrows of the people; fasting remains a personal choice
They are obligated to keep the full 24-hour fast and all the mourning restrictions as in Orthodox halacha
The day has been completely cancelled and is not mentioned anywhere
It is replaced only by a civil day off without Jewish meaning
questions.explanation: Classical nineteenth-century Reform often did not mourn the Temple; today many communities have restored this day as a day of remembrance and reflection.

questions.prompt: In many Reform communities in the Diaspora, Rosh Hashanah is celebrated for one day, not two.
questions.explanation: In this way they keep the Israeli length; the specific custom depends on the community.
questions.source: A lesson on the Days of Awe; calendar notes

questions.prompt: How, according to Judaism, is forgiveness attained on the Days of Awe?
options: By faith in someone else's atoning death
By teshuvah, tefillah, and tzedakah, without an intermediary
Only by an offering in the Temple, without which there is never forgiveness
By admitting an inborn guilt that a person cannot remove on his own
questions.explanation: The oral tradition of the Days of Awe: teshuvah, tefillah, and tzedakah. Hoshea 14:3 — “instead of bulls, the words of our lips.”
questions.source: Hoshea 14:3; Yechezkel 18:20; a lesson on the Days of Awe

questions.prompt: Yechezkel 18:20 teaches that a son bears his father's guilt and that guilt is passed on to everyone from birth.
questions.explanation: The opposite: “the son shall not bear the guilt of the father… the soul that sins — it shall die.” Each person answers for himself and can return.

questions.prompt: What is the Jewish meaning of the objects of the seder?
options: They are secret signs of a redeemer who has already come and of someone else's sacrifice
A remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt: matzah, the bitterness of slavery, the cups of redemption
A set of random customs with no connection to the Torah
Only a children's game; the seder has nothing to tell adults
questions.explanation: Mishnah Pesachim 10:5: a person is obligated to see himself as having come out of Egypt. The meaning of the seder is direct, not a cipher.

questions.prompt: In the Jewish tradition the seder is read as an open account of the Exodus, and not as a hidden hint of another event.
questions.explanation: The Haggadah speaks directly of the Exodus. Reinterpreting the evening as a set of secret signs diverges from the Jewish meaning of the festival.
questions.source: Mishnah Pesachim 10:5; a lesson on Pesach

questions.prompt: Besides the destruction of the Temples, what does one remember on Tisha B'Av when speaking of the Land?
options: Only the agricultural calendar
Exile from the Land and the hope of a complete return, including the Temple
The abolition of all the fasts, because the State already exists
Moving the capital away from Jerusalem
questions.explanation: Tisha B'Av is mourning for the exile and for the Temple. The people's return in our days is a consolation, but complete redemption is still ahead.
questions.source: Mishnah Ta'anit 4:6; a lesson on the fasts and on the Land

questions.prompt: Yom Yerushalayim marks the reunification of Jerusalem, the eternal and undivided capital of the Jewish people.
questions.explanation: On 28 Iyar 1967 the city was reunified. This course speaks of Jerusalem as the eternal capital, which is not divided.
questions.source: Lesson: Fasts and memorial days; Tehillim 137:5
